Full text

HOW TIDES ARE MADE

Twice a day, every day, the sea rises and falls along every shore in the world. The water comes in, and covers the beach, and then it goes out, and leaves the beach bare, and then it comes in again, and the rhythm never stops, and it has never stopped, for as long as there has been a sea and a moon. The tide is the most regular thing in nature, and it is also one of the most mysterious, because the force that makes it is invisible, and it comes from a quarter of a million miles away. The tide is made by the moon.

The moon pulls on the earth, and the earth pulls on the moon, and the pull is gravity, and gravity pulls everything, but it does not pull everything equally. The side of the earth that faces the moon is closer to the moon than the centre of the earth, and so it is pulled harder. The side of the earth that faces away from the moon is further from the moon than the centre, and so it is pulled less hard. The difference is small, but it is enough. The water on the near side is pulled toward the moon, and it piles up, and makes a bulge. The water on the far side is left behind, because the solid earth is pulled toward the moon more strongly than the water on the far side, and so the water on the far side piles up too, and makes a second bulge, on the opposite side of the earth. The earth has two bulges of water, one facing the moon, and one facing away from it, and the earth turns inside them, once a day, and every shore passes through both bulges, and that is why there are two high tides a day, and two low tides, and why the tide comes in, and goes out, and comes in again.

The sun makes tides too. The sun is much further away than the moon, and its pull is weaker, but it is not negligible. When the sun and the moon are in line — at the new moon and the full moon — their pulls add together, and the tides are higher, and lower, than usual. These are the spring tides, and they are called spring not because they happen in spring, but because the water springs up, higher than usual. When the sun and the moon are at right angles — at the first quarter and the last quarter — their pulls partly cancel, and the tides are smaller. These are the neap tides, and the difference between spring and neap is the difference between a tide that covers the whole beach and a tide that barely reaches the shore.

The tide is not the same everywhere. In some places, the tide rises a few inches. In others, it rises fifty feet. The difference is the shape of the shore. A bay that narrows toward its head will funnel the tide, and the water will pile up, higher and higher, as the bay narrows, until the tide at the head of the bay is many times higher than the tide at its mouth. A bay that is the right shape, and the right length, will resonate, like a pipe, and the tide will swing back and forth, growing larger with every swing, until it is enormous. The shape of the land makes the tide, as much as the moon does, and the tide is a partnership between the sky and the shore.

The tide does work. It carries ships in and out of harbour. It scours the channels, and keeps them deep. It brings food to the creatures of the shore, and it takes their waste away. It turns the mills, in the places where men have built tide mills, and it could turn more, if men chose to use it. The tide is a vast, regular, predictable source of energy, and it is free, and it will never run out, as long as the moon circles the earth, and the earth turns. The tide is the moon's gift to the sea, and the sea's gift to the shore, and the shore's gift to everyone who lives by it.

The tide is also a clock. The fishermen know it, and the sailors know it, and the people who live by the sea know it, because their lives are ruled by it. The boats go out on the ebb, and come in on the flood. The nets are set at low water, and hauled at high. The children play on the beach at low water, and come home before the flood. The tide tables are printed, and pinned up, in every harbour, and they are consulted, every day, like the weather, because the tide is the weather of the sea, and it must be known, or the sea will catch you out. A man who does not know the tide will be stranded, or drowned, or both, and the sea does not forgive ignorance.

The moon will go on making the tides, as long as it circles the earth, and the earth will go on turning inside the bulges, and the shores will go on rising and falling, twice a day, every day, for as long as there is a sea. The tide is the oldest rhythm in the world, older than the seasons, older than the day and the night, and it will outlast us all, and it will still be rising and falling, on shores where no one lives, long after we are gone. That is the tide: a bulge of water, pulled by the moon, shaped by the shore, and turning, twice a day, forever.

Men did not always know that the moon made the tides. For thousands of years, the tide was a mystery, and the explanations were many, and most of them were wrong. Some said the sea breathed, in and out, like a living thing. Some said the earth drank the sea, and gave it back. Some said the winds made the tide, and the tide followed the wind. It was Newton, in the seventeenth century, who showed that the tide was made by gravity, and that the moon's pull, differing from one side of the earth to the other, was enough to raise the water. Newton's explanation was a triumph, and it is still, in its essentials, the explanation we use today. The moon pulls, the water bulges, the earth turns, and the tide follows. It is a simple story, and it is true, and it is one of the great achievements of science: to take a mystery that had lasted for thousands of years, and to explain it with a single force, acting at a distance, across a quarter of a million miles of empty space.

The tide shapes the shore, and the shore shapes the life that lives on it. Between the high-water mark and the low-water mark is the intertidal zone, a strip of rock and sand that is covered twice a day and uncovered twice a day, and it is one of the hardest places in the world to live. The creatures that live there — the limpets, the barnacles, the mussels, the crabs, the anemones — must survive being underwater and being out of it, being battered by waves and being baked by the sun, being eaten by birds and being dried by the wind. They survive by clinging, and by closing, and by hiding, and by being tough in ways that few other creatures are. The rock pools, left behind by the ebb, are small worlds, full of life, and a child with a bucket and a net can find more living things in a single rock pool than in a whole field. The tide makes the pools, and the pools make the life, and the life makes the shore worth walking, at low water, with your eyes open.

Living with the tide means living by a clock that is not the clock on the wall. The tide's clock is the moon's clock, and the moon's day is twenty-four hours and fifty minutes, not twenty-four hours, because the moon moves in its orbit while the earth turns, and the tide comes fifty minutes later every day. The fisherman who goes out at dawn on Monday will go out fifty minutes later on Tuesday, and fifty minutes later again on Wednesday, and by the end of the week his dawn has moved by six hours, and he is going out at noon. The tide does not keep our hours. It keeps its own, and the people who live by it learn its hours, and they live by them, and the learning is a part of the life, and the life is shaped by it, as surely as the shore is shaped by the water.

The tide will be there tomorrow, and the day after, and the day after that, and it will be there when the children who play on the beach today are old, and it will be there when their children play on the same beach, and the rhythm will not change, because the moon will not change, and the sea will not change, and the turning of the earth will not change. The tide is the most reliable thing in the world, and it is free, and it is beautiful, and it is worth watching, at least once, from a shore, at the turn of the tide, when the water stops going out, and hangs, for a moment, still, and then begins to come in, and the beach that was bare is covered again, and the sea has kept its promise, as it always does, twice a day, every day, forever.

The tide has been put to work, and the work is worth describing, because it is the tide's most practical gift. The tide mill is an old device: a mill, built on the shore, with a pond behind it, and a gate in the wall. The tide comes in, and fills the pond, and the gate is closed, and the tide goes out, and the pond stays full, and the water is let out, through the mill wheel, and the wheel turns, and the mill grinds, and the grinding is done by the tide, and by nothing else. The tide mill is a machine that runs on the moon, and it has run, in places, for a thousand years, and it is still running, in a few places, because the moon has never failed to keep its appointment.

The modern form of the same idea is tidal power: a barrage, across an estuary, with turbines in it, that turn as the tide flows in, and as it flows out, and that make electricity, from the moon's pull, and from the sea's rise and fall. The power is predictable, because the tide is predictable, and it is clean, because the tide is clean, and it is large, because the tide is large, and the only cost is the building, and the building is large, and the argument about whether to build is an argument about the estuary, and the birds, and the fish, and the shore, and it is a real argument, and it should be had, carefully, before the building begins. The tide will give its power, to anyone who asks properly, and the asking properly means building in the right place, and in the right way, and the tide, like the sea, rewards respect, and punishes haste.

The earth has two bulges of water, one facing the moon, and one facing away from it, and the earth turns inside them, once a day, and every shore passes through both bulges, and that is why there are two high tides a day, and two low tides, and why the tide comes in, and goes out, and comes in again.\n\nThe sun makes tides too. The sun is much further away than the moon, and its pull is weaker, but it is not negligible. When the sun and the moon are in line — at the new moon and the full moon — their pulls add together, and the tides are higher, and lower, than usual. These are the spring tides, and they are called spring not because they happen in spring, but because the water springs up, higher than usual. When the sun and the moon are at right angles — at the first quarter and the last quarter — their pulls partly cancel, and the tides are smaller. These are the neap tides, and the difference between spring and neap is the difference between a tide that covers the whole beach and a tide that barely reaches the shore.\n\nThe tide is not the same everywhere. In some places, the tide rises a few inches. In others, it rises fifty feet. The difference is the shape of the shore. A bay that narrows toward its head will funnel the tide, and the water will pile up, higher and higher, as the bay narrows, until the tide at the head of the bay is many times higher than the tide at its mouth. A bay that is the right shape, and the right length, will resonate, like a pipe, and the tide will swing back and forth, growing larger with every swing, until it is enormous. The shape of the land makes the tide, as much as the moon does, and the tide is a partnership between the sky and the shore.\n\nThe tide does work. It carries ships in and out of harbour. It scours the channels, and keeps them deep. It brings food to the creatures of the shore, and it takes their waste away. It turns the mills, in the places where men have built tide mills, and it could turn more, if men chose to use it. The tide is a vast, regular, predictable source of energy, and it is free, and it will never run out, as long as the moon circles the earth, and the earth turns. The tide is the moon's gift to the sea, and the sea's gift to the shore, and the shore's gift to everyone who lives by it.\n\nThe tide is also a clock. The fishermen know it, and the sailors know it, and the people who live by the sea know it, because their lives are ruled by it. The boats go out on the ebb, and come in on the flood. The nets are set at low water, and hauled at high. The children play on the beach at low water, and come home before the flood. The tide tables are printed, and pinned up, in every harbour, and they are consulted, every day, like the weather, because the tide is the weather of the sea, and it must be known, or the sea will catch you out. For thousands of years, the tide was a mystery, and the explanations were many, and most of them were wrong. Some said the sea breathed, in and out, like a living thing. Some said the earth drank the sea, and gave it back. Some said the winds made the tide, and the tide followed the wind. It was Newton, in the seventeenth century, who showed that the tide was made by gravity, and that the moon's pull, differing from one side of the earth to the other, was enough to raise the water. THE MAKING OF A MAP

A map is a lie that tells the truth. It lies because it is flat, and the earth is round, and it lies because it is small, and the earth is large, and it lies because it leaves things out, and the earth leaves nothing out. It tells the truth because, in spite of the lies, it shows you where you are, and where you want to go, and how to get there, and that is the truth that matters. Making a map is the art of lying well: of choosing the lies that help, and refusing the lies that harm, and of drawing a picture of the world that a stranger can use to find his way.

The first step in making a map is the survey. A surveyor goes out, with instruments, and measures the land. He measures distances, with a chain, or with a tape, or with light. He measures angles, with a theodolite, an instrument that turns, and reads, with a precision that the eye cannot match. He measures heights, with a level, and a staff, and a knowledge of the sea's surface, which is the zero from which all heights are counted. He measures, and he writes the measurements down, and the measurements are the map's foundation, and the foundation must be right, because everything else is built on it, and a map built on wrong measurements is a map that will lead people astray, and a map that leads people astray is worse than no map at all.

The second step is the drawing. The surveyor, or the cartographer, takes the measurements, and turns them into a picture. The picture is drawn to a scale, and the scale is the map's contract with the reader: one inch on the map means one mile on the ground, or one inch means a thousand feet, or whatever the scale says, and the scale is written on the map, and the reader can trust it, and measure from it, and the measuring is the map's use. The drawing shows the roads, and the rivers, and the hills, and the towns, and the boundaries, and it shows them with symbols, and the symbols are a language, and the language must be learned, and the learning is easy, because the symbols are chosen to look like the things they mean: a blue line for a river, a brown line for a contour, a black square for a building, a red line for a main road. The map is a picture, and the picture is a language, and the language is the map's gift to the reader.

The third step is the choosing. A map cannot show everything. The earth has too much in it. The cartographer must choose what to show, and what to leave out, and the choosing is the art. A road map shows the roads, and leaves out the trees. A walking map shows the paths, and leaves out the motorways. A sea chart shows the water, and leaves out the land, except for the coast, which is the sailor's guide. The choosing is guided by the map's purpose, and the purpose is the question the map answers: how do I get there, where am I, what is here? A map that tries to answer every question answers none of them. A map that answers one question well is a good map.

The fourth step is the projection. The earth is round, and the map is flat, and the round cannot be made flat without stretching, or tearing, or both. The cartographer must choose a projection, a way of flattening the round earth, and every projection lies in some way. One projection keeps the shapes right, and distorts the sizes. Another keeps the sizes right, and distorts the shapes. Another keeps the directions right, and distorts everything else. The choice depends on the map's purpose: a sailor needs directions, and so he uses a projection that keeps directions true. A schoolchild needs shapes, and so she uses a projection that keeps shapes true. The projection is the map's deepest lie, and it is also its deepest truth, because the lie is chosen, and the choosing is honest, and the honesty is written on the map, in the form of the projection's name, for anyone who cares to look.

The map is printed, or drawn, and it is used, and the using is the test. A map that is used, and found true, is a good map. A map that is used, and found false, is a bad map, and it is corrected, or thrown away. The map is a tool, and tools are judged by their use, and the map's use is to show the way, and the way is the truth, and the truth is the map's purpose, and the purpose is the whole of it.

The mapmaker's work is never finished, because the world changes. Roads are built, and rivers change their course, and towns grow, and boundaries move, and the map must be revised, and the revision is the map's life. An old map is a history, and a new map is a promise, and the promise is that the world, as it is now, can be shown, and used, and understood, and the understanding is the map's gift, and the gift is worth the work, because the work is the making of a picture that a stranger can use to find his way, in a world that is round, and large, and full of things, and the picture is flat, and small, and full of choices, and the choices are the art, and the art is the map.

There is a pleasure in making a map by hand, with a pen and a straightedge, that no computer can give. The hand learns the land as it draws it, and the drawing is a kind of knowing, and the knowing is deeper than the reading. The cartographer who has drawn a coastline knows it, in a way that the man who has only looked at it does not. He knows its bays, and its points, and its rocks, because his hand has followed them, and the following is a kind of walking, and the walking is a kind of learning. The computer can draw a map faster, and more accurately, and in greater numbers, and it should, for the maps that must be made by the thousand. But the hand-drawn map has a quality that the computer map does not: it carries the maker's attention, and the attention is visible, in every line, and the visibility is the map's beauty.

The best maps are beautiful, and the beauty is not decoration. It is the sign of care. A map that is drawn with care is a map that can be trusted, because the care shows in the details: the lettering, even and clear; the symbols, consistent and true; the colours, chosen to help, not to dazzle; the empty spaces, left empty, because the cartographer does not know what is there, and will not invent it. The empty space on a map is the most honest thing on it. It says: we do not know. The old maps wrote "here be dragons" in the empty spaces, and the dragons were a joke, and a warning, and a promise: that the world is larger than the map, and that the map knows it, and that the knowing is the beginning of the next map.

So the map is a lie that tells the truth, and the making of it is the art of choosing the right lies. Choose the scale, and keep it. Choose the symbols, and keep them. Choose the projection, and name it. Choose what to show, and what to leave out, and leave the unknown blank. Do these things, and the map will serve the stranger who picks it up, and the stranger will find his way, and the way will be true, and the truth will be the map's reward, and the reward will be enough, because a map that shows the way is a map that has done its work, and the work is the whole of it.

The map for a child is a different thing from the map for a sailor, and it is worth making well, because the child who learns to read a map learns to read the world. The child's map is simple: few symbols, large lettering, bright colours, and a picture of the place that looks like the place, so that the child can find the park, and the school, and the home, and can see how they fit together. The child who can read a map of the neighbourhood can read a map of the town, and the child who can read a map of the town can read a map of the country, and the reading is a skill that grows with the reader, and that stays with the reader, for life. The map is a teacher, and the teaching is the finding of one's way, and the finding of one's way is the beginning of independence.

The map in the hand is a pleasure that the map on the screen cannot give. The paper map folds, and unfolds, and it can be spread on a table, and studied, and it shows the whole of the place at once, and the whole is the point, because the whole is what the screen cannot show. The screen shows a part, and the part moves, and the moving is useful, for finding one's way, but it is not the same as seeing the whole, and understanding how the parts fit. The paper map is a picture, and the picture can be held, and kept, and returned to, and the returning is the learning. The screen is a guide, and the guide is useful, and the picture is a map, and the map is better, for understanding, because it shows the whole, and the whole is the truth, and the truth is the map's gift.

Abstract

This study measured reading speed and comprehension across three text lengths — short (500 words), medium (2,000 words), and long (5,000 words) — in 120 adult readers. Mean reading speed was 248 words per minute for short texts, 241 for medium, and 233 for long. Mean comprehension was 8.4 out of 10 for short texts, 7.9 for medium, and 7.2 for long. The results suggest that length affects comprehension more than speed, and that the effect is driven by memory load rather than by reading rate.

Full text

READING SPEED AND COMPREHENSION ACROSS TEXT LENGTHS: A CONTROLLED STUDY

Abstract

This study measured reading speed and comprehension across three text lengths — short (500 words), medium (2,000 words), and long (5,000 words) — in 120 adult readers. Each participant read one text at each length, on matched topics, under timed conditions, and answered a ten-item comprehension test after each text. Mean reading speed was 248 words per minute for short texts, 241 for medium texts, and 233 for long texts, a small but reliable decline with length. Mean comprehension was 8.4 out of 10 for short texts, 7.9 for medium texts, and 7.2 for long texts, a larger decline. The results suggest that length affects comprehension more than speed, and that the effect is driven by memory load rather than by reading rate. The findings have practical implications for the design of reading materials, and for the teaching of reading.

1. Introduction

Reading is the most practised skill in the modern world, and it is also one of the least understood. Every day, millions of people read — books, newspapers, screens, signs — and every day, they read at different speeds, and understand different amounts, and no one can say, with confidence, why. The science of reading has measured many things: the movement of the eyes, the time taken to recognise a word, the effect of vocabulary, the effect of background knowledge. But one variable has received less attention than it deserves: the length of the text itself. Does a long text read differently from a short one? Does comprehension fall as the text grows? Does speed change? These are simple questions, and they matter, because the texts people read are getting longer, and shorter, at the same time — longer in books, shorter on screens — and the reader must cope with both.

The existing literature offers partial answers. Early work on reading established that reading speed, measured in words per minute, is relatively stable within an individual across texts of similar difficulty, and that comprehension, measured by questions answered correctly, declines when the text is difficult. But difficulty and length are not the same thing. A long text is not necessarily a difficult text, and a short text is not necessarily an easy one. The question of length, separated from difficulty, has been studied less, and the studies that exist disagree. Some find that speed falls with length, as readers tire. Some find that speed rises, as readers warm to the task. Some find no effect at all. The disagreement suggests that the effect, if it exists, is small, and that it depends on conditions that the studies did not control: the topic, the reader's interest, the time of day, the purpose of the reading.

This study was designed to control those conditions, and to answer three questions. First, does reading speed change with text length, when topic, difficulty, and purpose are held constant? Second, does comprehension change with text length, under the same conditions? Third, if both change, is the change in comprehension explained by the change in speed, or by something else — by the load on memory, for example, as the reader must hold more of the text in mind? The answers matter for anyone who writes, teaches, or designs reading material, because they tell us what length does to the reader, and what the reader can be expected to do with texts of different lengths.

The study's hypothesis was straightforward. Speed would decline slightly with length, as attention flagged. Comprehension would decline more, as the reader had to remember more, over a longer time, with more opportunities to forget. The decline in comprehension would be larger than the decline in speed, and it would be only partly explained by speed, because the main cause would be memory, not rate. The study was designed to test this hypothesis, and to measure the size of the effects, so that writers and teachers could plan accordingly.

1.1 Previous research

The earliest systematic work on reading speed and comprehension was done in the first decades of the twentieth century, when psychologists began to measure what readers actually do. Huey, in 1908, observed the movements of the eyes during reading, and showed that the eye does not move smoothly across the page, but jumps, in fixations, and that the mind reads during the fixations, not during the jumps. Thorndike, in 1917, showed that reading is reasoning: that the reader does not merely take in words, but weighs them, selects among them, and organises them, and that mistakes in reading are mistakes in reasoning, not mistakes in seeing. These two observations — that reading is discontinuous, and that it is active — have shaped every study since, including this one. A reader who reads a long text must make more jumps, and do more reasoning, and hold more of the result in mind, and the load grows with the length.

Later work refined the picture. Just and Carpenter, in 1980, proposed a theory in which the eye's fixations and the mind's comprehension are closely linked, and in which the time spent on a word reflects the work the mind is doing on it. Carver, in 1990, reviewed the research on reading rate, and distinguished five rates — scanning, skimming, normal reading, learning, and memorising — and showed that the rate a reader adopts depends on the purpose, and that the purpose is set by the task, not by the text. Rayner, in 1998, reviewed twenty years of eye-movement research, and showed that the average fixation lasts about 200 to 250 milliseconds, and that the average reader makes about four fixations a second, and that these figures are stable across texts, but that the number of fixations, and the number of regressions — the backward jumps, when the reader goes back to re-read — grows with the difficulty of the text, and with its length.

The length question itself has been addressed directly, but rarely in isolation. Studies that varied length usually varied difficulty at the same time, by using different texts, on different topics, at different levels, so that the effect of length could not be separated from the effect of difficulty. Studies that held difficulty constant usually used texts that were short, because short texts are easier to match, and the range of lengths studied was narrow — from a few hundred words to a thousand or two. The present study extends the range to five thousand words, and holds topic, difficulty, and style constant across three lengths, so that the effect of length, and length alone, can be measured. It is, so far as the author knows, the first study to do so over this range, with this degree of control.

The study also addresses a practical question that the literature has left open: whether the comprehension loss in long texts is a matter of speed or of memory. If it is a matter of speed — if readers read long texts faster, and faster reading means shallower reading — then the remedy is to slow down. If it is a matter of memory — if readers read at the same speed, but forget more, because there is more to hold — then the remedy is different: it is to support the memory, with structure, and with aids. The study was designed to distinguish these two accounts, by measuring both speed and comprehension, and by testing whether the comprehension effect survives when speed is controlled.

2. Methods

2.1 Participants

One hundred and twenty adults took part in the study, sixty women and sixty men, aged between eighteen and sixty-five, with a mean age of thirty-four. All were native speakers of English, and all had completed at least twelve years of education. None reported a reading difficulty, and none wore glasses that corrected their vision to less than normal. Participants were recruited from the local community, through notices in libraries and community centres, and were paid a small fee for their time. Each participant attended a single session, lasting about ninety minutes, in a quiet room, with a desk, a chair, and a lamp.

2.2 Materials

Three texts were prepared for the study, one at each length: short (500 words), medium (2,000 words), and long (5,000 words). All three texts were on the same general topic — the history of the lighthouse — and all three were written by the same author, in the same style, at the same reading level, so that difficulty was held constant across lengths. The short text was a complete account, in miniature. The medium text was a fuller account, with more detail and more examples. The long text was the fullest account, with the most detail, the most examples, and the most digression. The three texts were not the same text cut to different lengths; they were three complete texts, on the same topic, at different lengths, so that each was a natural reading experience, and none was a fragment.

Each text was followed by a comprehension test of ten questions. The questions were of three kinds: four questions about facts stated in the text, three questions about inferences that followed from the text, and three questions about the text's structure — its main idea, its organisation, its purpose. The questions were the same in form across the three texts, and they were written to the same difficulty, so that a score on one test could be compared with a score on another. The tests were printed on separate sheets, and were given after the reading, without the text present, so that the test measured memory and understanding, not the ability to look back.

2.3 Procedure

Each participant read all three texts, in a counterbalanced order, so that one third read the short text first, one third read the medium text first, and one third read the long text first. The order was assigned by the experimenter, before the session, and the participant did not know the order in advance. Each text was presented on paper, in a folder, and the participant was told to read it at a normal pace, as if reading for pleasure, and to turn the page when ready. The experimenter timed the reading, with a stopwatch, from the moment the participant opened the folder to the moment the participant closed it. The participant was then given the comprehension test, and was told to answer all ten questions, without returning to the text. The participant then rested for five minutes, and read the next text. The session ended with a short questionnaire, asking the participant about their reading habits, and their interest in the topic.

2.4 Analysis

Reading speed was calculated as the number of words in the text divided by the time taken to read it, in minutes, giving words per minute. Comprehension was calculated as the number of questions answered correctly, out of ten. The data were analysed by repeated-measures analysis of variance, with text length as the within-participants factor, and with reading order as a between-participants factor, to check for order effects. The relationship between speed and comprehension was examined by correlation, within each length, and across lengths. The level of significance was set at p < .05, and all tests were two-tailed.

3. Results

3.1 Reading speed

Mean reading speed declined with text length. For short texts, the mean speed was 248 words per minute (standard deviation 31). For medium texts, the mean speed was 241 words per minute (standard deviation 29). For long texts, the mean speed was 233 words per minute (standard deviation 33). The decline from short to long was 15 words per minute, or 6 per cent. Analysis of variance showed a significant main effect of length on speed, F(2, 238) = 8.41, p < .001. Pairwise comparisons showed that the short text was read significantly faster than the long text (p < .001), and the medium text was read significantly faster than the long text (p = .02), but the short and medium texts did not differ significantly (p = .11). Reading order had no significant effect on speed, F(2, 117) = 0.62, p = .54, and there was no interaction between order and length, F(4, 234) = 0.91, p = .46.

3.2 Comprehension

Mean comprehension declined more steeply with length. For short texts, the mean score was 8.4 out of 10 (standard deviation 1.1). For medium texts, the mean score was 7.9 (standard deviation 1.3). For long texts, the mean score was 7.2 (standard deviation 1.5). The decline from short to long was 1.2 points, or 12 per cent of the scale. Analysis of variance showed a significant main effect of length on comprehension, F(2, 238) = 31.27, p < .001. All pairwise comparisons were significant: short better than medium (p = .003), medium better than long (p < .001), short better than long (p < .001). Reading order had no significant effect on comprehension, F(2, 117) = 0.44, p = .65, and there was no interaction between order and length, F(4, 234) = 1.12, p = .35.

3.3 Speed and comprehension

Within each length, speed and comprehension were weakly and negatively correlated: faster readers understood slightly less, but the relationship was small (short: r = -.18, p = .04; medium: r = -.21, p = .02; long: r = -.24, p = .008). Across lengths, the decline in comprehension was larger than the decline in speed, and the two declines were not proportional: speed fell by 6 per cent from short to long, while comprehension fell by 14 per cent. A mediation analysis showed that speed accounted for only a small part of the comprehension decline. When speed was controlled statistically, the effect of length on comprehension remained significant, F(2, 237) = 24.63, p < .001, and the size of the effect was reduced by only 18 per cent. The remaining 82 per cent of the length effect on comprehension was independent of speed.

3.4 Question types

The comprehension decline was not uniform across question types. Fact questions showed the smallest decline: 3.6 out of 4 for short texts, 3.4 for medium, 3.2 for long. Inference questions showed a larger decline: 2.6 out of 3 for short, 2.4 for medium, 2.1 for long. Structure questions showed the largest decline: 2.2 out of 3 for short, 2.1 for medium, 1.9 for long. The pattern suggests that length affects the reader's grasp of the text as a whole — its argument, its organisation, its purpose — more than it affects the reader's memory for individual facts.

3.5 Reading habits

The questionnaire, given at the end of the session, asked participants about their reading habits: how many books they read in a year, how many hours a week they spent reading, and whether they read mostly books, or mostly screens. The answers varied widely. The mean number of books read in a year was 14, with a range from 0 to 80. The mean hours spent reading per week was 6, with a range from 0 to 25. Fifty-eight per cent of participants said they read mostly books, 29 per cent said they read mostly screens, and 13 per cent said they read both equally.

Reading habits were related to both speed and comprehension, but the relationships were modest. The number of books read in a year correlated with reading speed (r = .31, p < .001) and with comprehension (r = .28, p = .002). The hours spent reading per week correlated with speed (r = .26, p = .004) and with comprehension (r = .24, p = .008). The readers who read more, read faster, and understood more, but the advantage was small, and it did not remove the length effect: when reading habits were controlled statistically, the effect of length on comprehension remained significant, F(2, 236) = 29.84, p < .001, and the size of the effect was reduced by only 6 per cent. The length effect is not a matter of being a good reader, or a practised reader. It is a matter of length, and it affects the practised reader, and the unpractised reader, alike.

The screen readers, who read mostly on screens, were faster than the book readers, by a mean of 12 words per minute, but they understood less, by a mean of 0.4 points out of 10, and the difference in comprehension was significant (t = 2.31, p = .02), while the difference in speed was not (t = 1.42, p = .16). The finding is consistent with the literature, which suggests that screen reading encourages skimming, and that skimming costs comprehension, and it is a reminder that the medium matters, as well as the length, and that the two should be studied together, in future work.

4. Discussion

The study found that text length affects both reading speed and comprehension, but affects comprehension more. Speed fell by 6 per cent from a 500-word text to a 5,000-word text. Comprehension fell by 14 per cent over the same range. The difference in size is the study's central finding, and it points to memory, not rate, as the main mechanism. If comprehension fell only because readers read faster, and faster reading meant less careful reading, then the two declines would be proportional, and controlling for speed would remove the length effect. It did not. Four fifths of the length effect on comprehension remained after speed was controlled. Something else is doing the work, and the most likely candidate is memory load: the longer the text, the more the reader must hold in mind, and the more there is to forget.

The question-type analysis supports this interpretation. Fact questions, which depend on remembering a single detail, declined least. Structure questions, which depend on holding the whole text in mind, declined most. A reader can remember a fact from the beginning of a long text, if the fact is striking, but it is harder to remember how the text as a whole is organised, when the organisation must be held in mind across five thousand words. The long text is not harder to read, word by word. It is harder to hold, as a whole, and the holding is the work of memory, and memory is limited.

The practical implications are straightforward. Writers of long texts should help the reader's memory. Headings, summaries, signposts, and recapitulations are not decorations; they are memory aids, and they matter more in long texts than in short ones, because the memory load is greater. Teachers should teach readers to use them: to pause, to summarise, to note the structure, to return to the beginning. And readers should know that a long text will cost them comprehension, even if they read it at the same speed, and that the cost can be paid in attention, if they choose to pay it.

The study has limits, and they should be stated plainly. The texts were all on the same topic, and the topic was chosen to be interesting but not familiar. A topic the reader knows well might show a smaller length effect, because prior knowledge reduces the memory load. A topic the reader finds boring might show a larger effect, because attention flags sooner. The participants were adults, reading on paper, in a quiet room. Reading on a screen, or in a noisy room, or under time pressure, might show different effects. The study measured immediate comprehension, not delayed recall, and the length effect on delayed recall might be larger still, or smaller. These are questions for further research, and the study's design — three lengths, matched topics, counterbalanced order — can be reused for them.

4.1 Implications for teaching and design

The findings have direct implications for three groups: writers, teachers, and readers. For writers, the implication is that length is a cost, and the cost should be paid deliberately. A long text should earn its length, by giving the reader what a short text cannot: more evidence, more examples, more nuance. A long text that merely repeats itself, or that wanders, will cost the reader comprehension without giving anything in return. The writer of a long text should also build in the devices that support memory. A heading every few hundred words, a summary at the end of each section, a sentence that says what has been shown and what comes next — these are not concessions to the inattentive reader. They are the tools that let the attentive reader hold the text whole. The study suggests that these devices matter more as length grows, and that a long text without them is a text that asks the reader to do the writer's work.

For teachers, the implication is that reading instruction should include the long text as a skill in its own right. The skills that serve a short text — reading carefully, answering questions, remembering facts — do not, by themselves, serve a long text. The long text requires additional skills: skimming for structure, noting the argument, summarising as one goes, returning to the beginning. These skills can be taught, and they should be taught explicitly, with long texts, in the classroom, where the teacher can show the student how to hold a five-thousand-word argument in mind. The study's question-type analysis gives the teacher a guide: the facts will look after themselves, more or less. It is the structure that needs teaching, because the structure is what the length takes away.

For readers, the implication is simpler, and it is a matter of self-knowledge. A reader who knows that a long text will cost comprehension can plan for it: read in sessions, not in one sitting; pause, and summarise; note the structure; return to the beginning when lost. The reader who does not know will blame himself for the loss, or blame the text, and neither blame is correct. The loss is a property of length, and of memory, and it can be managed, once it is understood. The reader's task is not to read faster, or to read more carefully, in the abstract. It is to read in a way that fits the length, and the way that fits a long text is a way that supports the memory, at every step.

5. Conclusion

Text length affects reading, and it affects comprehension more than speed. A reader who moves from a 500-word text to a 5,000-word text will read only slightly more slowly, but will understand measurably less, and the loss will be greatest for the text's overall structure and purpose. The loss is not explained by speed. It is explained, most plausibly, by memory load, and it can be reduced by the devices that support memory: headings, summaries, and signposts. Writers, teachers, and readers should plan for the length effect, and should treat the long text not as a short text extended, but as a different kind of reading, with different demands, and different needs.

References

Carver, R. P. Reading Rate: A Review of Research and Theory. San Diego: Academic Press, 1990.
Huey, E. B. The Psychology and Pedagogy of Reading. New York: Macmillan, 1908.
Just, M. A., and Carpenter, P. A. "A Theory of Reading: From Eye Fixations to Comprehension." Psychological Review 87 (1980), pp. 329-354.
Rayner, K. "Eye Movements in Reading and Information Processing: 20 Years of Research." Psychological Bulletin 124 (1998), pp. 372-422.
Thorndike, E. L. "Reading as Reasoning: A Study of Mistakes in Paragraph Reading." Journal of Educational Psychology 8 (1917), pp. 323-332.

Fact questions showed the smallest decline: 3.6 out of 4 for short texts, 3.4 for medium, 3.2 for long. Inference questions showed a larger decline: 2.6 out of 3 for short, 2.4 for medium, 2.1 for long. Structure questions showed the largest decline: 2.2 out of 3 for short, 2.1 for medium, 1.9 for long. The pattern suggests that length affects the reader\'s grasp of the text as a whole — its argument, its organisation, its purpose — more than it affects the reader\'s memory for individual facts.\n\n3.5 Reading habits\n\nThe questionnaire, given at the end of the session, asked participants about their reading habits: how many books they read in a year, how many hours a week they spent reading, and whether they read mostly books, or mostly screens. The answers varied widely. The mean number of books read in a year was 14, with a range from 0 to 80. The mean hours spent reading per week was 6, with a range from 0 to 25. Fifty-eight per cent of participants said they read mostly books, 29 per cent said they read mostly screens, and 13 per cent said they read both equally.\n\nReading habits were related to both speed and comprehension, but the relationships were modest. The number of books read in a year correlated with reading speed (r = .31, p < .001) and with comprehension (r = .28, p = .002). The hours spent reading per week correlated with speed (r = .26, p = .004) and with comprehension (r = .24, p = .008). The readers who read more, read faster, and understood more, but the advantage was small, and it did not remove the length effect: when reading habits were controlled statistically, the effect of length on comprehension remained significant, F(2, 236) = 29.84, p < .001, and the size of the effect was reduced by only 6 per cent. The length effect is not a matter of being a good reader, or a practised reader. It is a matter of length, and it affects the practised reader, and the unpractised reader, alike.\n\nThe screen readers, who read mostly on screens, were faster than the book readers, by a mean of 12 words per minute, but they understood less, by a mean of 0.4 points out of 10, and the difference in comprehension was significant (t = 2.31, p = .02), while the difference in speed was not (t = 1.42, p = .16). The finding is consistent with the literature, which suggests that screen reading encourages skimming, and that skimming costs comprehension, and it is a reminder that the medium matters, as well as the length, and that the two should be studied together, in future work.\n\n4. Discussion\n\nThe study found that text length affects both reading speed and comprehension, but affects comprehension more. Speed fell by 6 per cent from a 500-word text to a 5,000-word text. Comprehension fell by 14 per cent over the same range. The difference in size is the study\'s central finding, and it points to memory, not rate, as the main mechanism. If comprehension fell only because readers read faster, and faster reading meant less careful reading, then the two declines would be proportional, and controlling for speed would remove the length effect. It did not. Four fifths of the length effect on comprehension remained after speed was controlled. Something else is doing the work, and the most likely candidate is memory load: the longer the text, the more the reader must hold in mind, and the more there is to forget.\n\nThe question-type analysis supports this interpretation. Fact questions, which depend on remembering a single detail, declined least. Structure questions, which depend on holding the whole text in mind, declined most. A reader can remember a fact from the beginning of a long text, if the fact is striking, but it is harder to remember how the text as a whole is organised, when the organisation must be held in mind across five thousand words. The long text is not harder to read, word by word. It is harder to hold, as a whole, and the holding is the work of memory, and memory is limited.\n\nThe practical implications are straightforward. Writers of long texts should help the reader\'s memory. Headings, summaries, signposts, and recapitulations are not decorations; they are memory aids, and they matter more in long texts than in short ones, because the memory load is greater. Teachers should teach readers to use them: to pause, to summarise, to note the structure, to return to the beginning. And readers should know that a long text will cost them comprehension, even if they read it at the same speed, and that the cost can be paid in attention, if they choose to pay it.\n\nThe study has limits, and they should be stated plainly. The texts were all on the same topic, and the topic was chosen to be interesting but not familiar. A topic the reader knows well might show a smaller length effect, because prior knowledge reduces the memory load. A topic the reader finds boring might show a larger effect, because attention flags sooner. The participants were adults, reading on paper, in a quiet room. Reading on a screen, or in a noisy room, or under time pressure, might show different effects. The study measured immediate comprehension, not delayed recall, and the length effect on delayed recall might be larger still, or smaller. These are questions for further research, and the study\'s design — three lengths, matched topics, counterbalanced order — can be reused for them.\n\n4.1 Implications for teaching and design\n\nThe findings have direct implications for three groups: writers, teachers, and readers. For writers, the implication is that length is a cost, and the cost should be paid deliberately. A long text should earn its length, by giving the reader what a short text cannot: more evidence, more examples, more nuance. A long text that merely repeats itself, or that wanders, will cost the reader comprehension without giving anything in return. The writer of a long text should also build in the devices that support memory. A heading every few hundred words, a summary at the end of each section, a sentence that says what has been shown and what comes next — these are not concessions to the inattentive reader. They are the tools that let the attentive reader hold the text whole. The study suggests that these devices matter more as length grows, and that a long text without them is a text that asks the reader to do the writer\'s work.\n\nFor teachers, the implication is that reading instruction should include the long text as a skill in its own right. The skills that serve a short text — reading carefully, answering questions, remembering facts — do not, by themselves, serve a long text. The long text requires additional skills: skimming for structure, noting the argument, summarising as one goes, returning to the beginning. These skills can be taught, and they should be taught explicitly, with long texts, in the classroom, where the teacher can show the student how to hold a five-thousand-word argument in mind. The study\'s question-type analysis gives the teacher a guide: the facts will look after themselves, more or less. It is the structure that needs teaching, because the structure is what the length takes away.\n\nFor readers, the implication is simpler, and it is a matter of self-knowledge. A reader who knows that a long text will cost comprehension can plan for it: read in sessions, not in one sitting; pause, and summarise; note the structure; return to the beginning when lost. The reader who does not know will blame himself for the loss, or blame the text, and neither blame is correct. The loss is a property of length, and of memory, and it can be managed, once it is understood. The reader\'s task is not to read faster, or to read more carefully, in the abstract. It is to read in a way that fits the length, and the way that fits a long text is a way that supports the memory, at every step.\n\n5. Conclusion\n\nText length affects reading, and it affects comprehension more than speed. A reader who moves from a 500-word text to a 5,000-word text will read only slightly more slowly, but will understand measurably less, and the loss will be greatest for the text\'s overall structure and purpose. The loss is not explained by speed. It is explained, most plausibly, by memory load, and it can be reduced by the devices that support memory: headings, summaries, and signposts. Writers, teachers, and readers should plan for the length effect, and should treat the long text not as a short text extended, but as a different kind of reading, with different demands, and different needs.\n\nReferences\n\nCarver, R. TEXT = 'READING SPEED AND COMPREHENSION ACROSS TEXT LENGTHS: A CONTROLLED STUDY\n\nAbstract\n\nThis study measured reading speed and comprehension across three text lengths — short (500 words), medium (2,000 words), and long (5,000 words) — in 120 adult readers. Each participant read one text at each length, on matched topics, under timed conditions, and answered a ten-item comprehension test after each text. Mean reading speed was 248 words per minute for short texts, 241 for medium texts, and 233 for long texts, a small but reliable decline with length. Mean comprehension was 8.4 out of 10 for short texts, 7.9 for medium texts, and 7.2 for long texts, a larger decline. The results suggest that length affects comprehension more than speed, and that the effect is driven by memory load rather than by reading rate. The findings have practical implications for the design of reading materials, and for the teaching of reading.\n\n1. Introduction\n\nReading is the most practised skill in the modern world, and it is also one of the least understood. Every day, millions of people read — books, newspapers, screens, signs — and every day, they read at different speeds, and understand different amounts, and no one can say, with confidence, why. The science of reading has measured many things: the movement of the eyes, the time taken to recognise a word, the effect of vocabulary, the effect of background knowledge. But one variable has received less attention than it deserves: the length of the text itself. Does a long text read differently from a short one? Does comprehension fall as the text grows? Does speed change? These are simple questions, and they matter, because the texts people read are getting longer, and shorter, at the same time — longer in books, shorter on screens — and the reader must cope with both.\n\nThe existing literature offers partial answers. Early work on reading established that reading speed, measured in words per minute, is relatively stable within an individual across texts of similar difficulty, and that comprehension, measured by questions answered correctly, declines when the text is difficult. But difficulty and length are not the same thing. A long text is not necessarily a difficult text, and a short text is not necessarily an easy one. The question of length, separated from difficulty, has been studied less, and the studies that exist disagree. Some find that speed falls with length, as readers tire. Some find that speed rises, as readers warm to the task. Some find no effect at all. The disagreement suggests that the effect, if it exists, is small, and that it depends on conditions that the studies did not control: the topic, the reader\'s interest, the time of day, the purpose of the reading.\n\nThis study was designed to control those conditions, and to answer three questions. First, does reading speed change with text length, when topic, difficulty, and purpose are held constant? Second, does comprehension change with text length, under the same conditions? Third, if both change, is the change in comprehension explained by the change in speed, or by something else — by the load on memory, for example, as the reader must hold more of the text in mind? The answers matter for anyone who writes, teaches, or designs reading material, because they tell us what length does to the reader, and what the reader can be expected to do with texts of different lengths.\n\nThe study\'s hypothesis was straightforward. Speed would decline slightly with length, as attention flagged. Comprehension would decline more, as the reader had to remember more, over a longer time, with more opportunities to forget. The decline in comprehension would be larger than the decline in speed, and it would be only partly explained by speed, because the main cause would be memory, not rate. The study was designed to test this hypothesis, and to measure the size of the effects, so that writers and teachers could plan accordingly.\n\n1.1 Previous research\n\nThe earliest systematic work on reading speed and comprehension was done in the first decades of the twentieth century, when psychologists began to measure what readers actually do. Huey, in 1908, observed the movements of the eyes during reading, and showed that the eye does not move smoothly across the page, but jumps, in fixations, and that the mind reads during the fixations, not during the jumps. Thorndike, in 1917, showed that reading is reasoning: that the reader does not merely take in words, but weighs them, selects among them, and organises them, and that mistakes in reading are mistakes in reasoning, not mistakes in seeing. These two observations — that reading is discontinuous, and that it is active — have shaped every study since, including this one. A reader who reads a long text must make more jumps, and do more reasoning, and hold more of the result in mind, and the load grows with the length.\n\nLater work refined the picture. Just and Carpenter, in 1980, proposed a theory in which the eye\'s fixations and the mind\'s comprehension are closely linked, and in which the time spent on a word reflects the work the mind is doing on it. Carver, in 1990, reviewed the research on reading rate, and distinguished five rates — scanning, skimming, normal reading, learning, and memorising — and showed that the rate a reader adopts depends on the purpose, and that the purpose is set by the task, not by the text. Rayner, in 1998, reviewed twenty years of eye-movement research, and showed that the average fixation lasts about 200 to 250 milliseconds, and that the average reader makes about four fixations a second, and that these figures are stable across texts, but that the number of fixations, and the number of regressions — the backward jumps, when the reader goes back to re-read — grows with the difficulty of the text, and with its length.\n\nThe length question itself has been addressed directly, but rarely in isolation. Studies that varied length usually varied difficulty at the same time, by using different texts, on different topics, at different levels, so that the effect of length could not be separated from the effect of difficulty. Studies that held difficulty constant usually used texts that were short, because short texts are easier to match, and the range of lengths studied was narrow — from a few hundred words to a thousand or two. The present study extends the range to five thousand words, and holds topic, difficulty, and style constant across three lengths, so that the effect of length, and length alone, can be measured. It is, so far as the author knows, the first study to do so over this range, with this degree of control.\n\nThe study also addresses a practical question that the literature has left open: whether the comprehension loss in long texts is a matter of speed or of memory. If it is a matter of speed — if readers read long texts faster, and faster reading means shallower reading — then the remedy is to slow down. If it is a matter of memory — if readers read at the same speed, but forget more, because there is more to hold — then the remedy is different: it is to support the memory, with structure, and with aids. The study was designed to distinguish these two accounts, by measuring both speed and comprehension, and by testing whether the comprehension effect survives when speed is controlled.\n\n2. Methods\n\n2.1 Participants\n\nOne hundred and twenty adults took part in the study, sixty women and sixty men, aged between eighteen and sixty-five, with a mean age of thirty-four. All were native speakers of English, and all had completed at least twelve years of education. None reported a reading difficulty, and none wore glasses that corrected their vision to less than normal. Participants were recruited from the local community, through notices in libraries and community centres, and were paid a small fee for their time. Each participant attended a single session, lasting about ninety minutes, in a quiet room, with a desk, a chair, and a lamp.\n\n2.2 Materials\n\nThree texts were prepared for the study, one at each length: short (500 words), medium (2,000 words), and long (5,000 words). All three texts were on the same general topic — the history of the lighthouse — and all three were written by the same author, in the same style, at the same reading level, so that difficulty was held constant across lengths. The short text was a complete account, in miniature. The medium text was a fuller account, with more detail and more examples. The long text was the fullest account, with the most detail, the most examples, and the most digression. The three texts were not the same text cut to different lengths; they were three complete texts, on the same topic, at different lengths, so that each was a natural reading experience, and none was a fragment.\n\nEach text was followed by a comprehension test of ten questions. The questions were of three kinds: four questions about facts stated in the text, three questions about inferences that followed from the text, and three questions about the text\'s structure — its main idea, its organisation, its purpose. The questions were the same in form across the three texts, and they were written to the same difficulty, so that a score on one test could be compared with a score on another. The tests were printed on separate sheets, and were given after the reading, without the text present, so that the test measured memory and understanding, not the ability to look back.\n\n2.3 Procedure\n\nEach participant read all three texts, in a counterbalanced order, so that one third read the short text first, one third read the medium text first, and one third read the long text first. The order was assigned by the experimenter, before the session, and the participant did not know the order in advance. Each text was presented on paper, in a folder, and the participant was told to read it at a normal pace, as if reading for pleasure, and to turn the page when ready. The experimenter timed the reading, with a stopwatch, from the moment the participant opened the folder to the moment the participant closed it. The participant was then given the comprehension test, and was told to answer all ten questions, without returning to the text. The participant then rested for five minutes, and read the next text. The session ended with a short questionnaire, asking the participant about their reading habits, and their interest in the topic.\n\n2.4 Analysis\n\nReading speed was calculated as the number of words in the text divided by the time taken to read it, in minutes, giving words per minute. Comprehension was calculated as the number of questions answered correctly, out of ten. The data were analysed by repeated-measures analysis of variance, with text length as the within-participants factor, and with reading order as a between-participants factor, to check for order effects. Writers, teachers, and readers should plan for the length effect, and should treat the long text not as a short text extended, but as a different kind of reading, with different demands, and different needs.\n\nReferences\n\nCarver, R.
