SLEEP DURATION AND NEXT-DAY RECALL OF WORD LISTS: AN EXPERIMENTAL STUDY

Abstract

This study tested whether the duration of a night's sleep affects the recall, the next day, of word lists learned the evening before. Ninety adults learned a list of forty unrelated words, and were then assigned to one of three sleep conditions: a full night (eight hours in bed), a short night (four hours in bed), or no sleep. Recall was tested twelve hours after learning, by free recall and by cued recall. The full-night group recalled a mean of 24.6 words by free recall, the short-night group 19.8, and the no-sleep group 15.3. Cued recall showed the same pattern, at higher levels. The results show a clear dose-response relationship between sleep duration and memory, and they support the view that sleep consolidates memory, and that the consolidation depends on the amount of sleep obtained. The findings have implications for students, for shift workers, and for anyone who must remember what was learned the day before.

1. Introduction

Everyone knows that a good night's sleep helps the memory, and that a bad night hurts it. The student who stays up all night before an examination knows it, and the student who sleeps knows it too, and both act on what they know, or fail to act on it, as the case may be. But knowing that sleep helps is not the same as knowing how much it helps, or how much sleep is needed, or whether the help depends on the length of the sleep, or on its depth, or on its timing. These are questions for experiment, and the experiment reported here is a simple one: learn a list of words, sleep for eight hours, or four hours, or not at all, and see how many words you remember the next day.

The question is old. Ebbinghaus, in 1885, measured the forgetting of nonsense syllables over time, and showed that forgetting is rapid at first, and slower later, and that the curve of forgetting is a law of memory. He did not study sleep, but his work made the study of sleep possible, because it gave the field a method: learn something, wait, and test. Jenkins and Dallenbach, in 1924, used that method to compare forgetting during sleep and during waking, and found that material learned before sleep was forgotten more slowly than material learned before a period of waking. Their finding — that sleep protects memory — has been confirmed many times since, and it is now one of the most reliable findings in the science of memory.

The modern work has gone further. It has shown that sleep does not merely protect memory from interference, but actively consolidates it: that during sleep, the brain replays what was learned, and strengthens it, and integrates it with what is already known. The work of Walker and his colleagues, and of Diekelmann and Born, has shown that the consolidation depends on the stages of sleep — on slow-wave sleep, in the first part of the night, and on rapid-eye-movement sleep, in the second — and that different kinds of memory depend on different stages. Declarative memory, the memory for facts and words, depends most on slow-wave sleep. Procedural memory, the memory for skills, depends most on rapid-eye-movement sleep. The word list, which is a test of declarative memory, should therefore benefit most from the first part of the night, and from the slow-wave sleep it contains.

But the dose-response question — how much sleep is enough, and how much is lost when sleep is cut short — has been studied less. Most studies compare sleep with no sleep, or a full night with a night cut in half, and they find a difference, but they do not map the curve. This study maps the curve, at three points: eight hours, four hours, and no sleep. The hypothesis was that recall would decline with sleep duration, in an orderly way, and that the decline would be larger for free recall than for cued recall, because free recall depends more on the strength of the memory trace, and cued recall gives the reader a hint, and the hint compensates for a weaker trace. The study was also designed to test whether the effect was the same for all participants, or whether it depended on age, or on habitual sleep, or on the time of learning.

1.1 Previous research

Ebbinghaus's work, in 1885, is the foundation. He learned lists of nonsense syllables, and tested himself, at intervals, and plotted the results, and the curve he found — steep at first, then flattening — is still the standard description of forgetting. His method, of learning to a criterion and testing after a delay, is the method used here, with real words instead of nonsense syllables, because real words are what people need to remember, in life, and the study was designed to be practical, as well as scientific.

Jenkins and Dallenbach, in 1924, made the first direct comparison of sleep and waking. They had participants learn nonsense syllables, and then either sleep or stay awake, for one, two, four, or eight hours, and then recall them. The sleepers forgot less, at every interval, and the difference grew with time. Their study is the ancestor of this one, and the present study repeats its design, with three changes: real words instead of nonsense syllables, a fixed twelve-hour delay, and three sleep durations, so that the dose-response curve can be mapped.

The modern consolidation literature adds the mechanism. Diekelmann and Born, in 2010, reviewed the evidence that sleep consolidates memory, and proposed that the consolidation is an active process, in which the hippocampus replays the day's learning during slow-wave sleep, and transfers it to the neocortex, for long-term storage. Walker, in 2005, and in later work, showed that sleep deprivation impairs the formation of new memories, as well as the retention of old ones, and that the impairment is proportional to the loss of sleep. The present study is consistent with this literature, and it tests a prediction that follows from it: that the amount of consolidation, and therefore the amount recalled, should depend on the amount of sleep, and should decline, in an orderly way, as sleep is shortened.

2. Methods

2.1 Participants

Ninety adults took part in the study, forty-five women and forty-five men, aged between eighteen and forty, with a mean age of twenty-six. All were native speakers of English, and all reported sleeping between seven and nine hours a night, habitually. None reported a sleep disorder, and none was taking medication that affected sleep. Participants were recruited from the local community, through notices in libraries and community centres, and were paid a small fee. Each participant attended two sessions: an evening learning session, and a morning test session, twelve hours later.

2.2 Materials

The learning material was a list of forty unrelated English nouns, chosen to be concrete, familiar, and of similar frequency in the language. The words were: table, river, candle, garden, hammer, window, bridge, pillow, anchor, feather, kettle, valley, pocket, ladder, mirror, needle, saddle, basket, chimney, island, button, carpet, dagger, engine, forest, guitar, harbour, lantern, magnet, napkin, orchard, palace, quarry, ribbon, tunnel, temple, umbrella, village, wallet, yarn, and zebra. Each word was printed on a separate card, in large type, and the cards were presented in a fixed order, which was the same for all participants.

2.3 Procedure

The learning session began at 8 p.m. Each participant was shown the forty cards, one at a time, for five seconds each, and was asked to read the word aloud, and to try to remember it. After all forty cards had been shown, the participant was given a five-minute break, and then was tested, by free recall, to establish a baseline: the participant wrote down as many of the forty words as could be remembered, in any order, in two minutes. The baseline was used to check that the groups were matched, and it was not counted in the results. After the baseline test, the participant was assigned to one of three sleep conditions, by random allocation, thirty participants to each condition.

The full-night group went to bed at 10 p.m., in the sleep laboratory, and was woken at 6 a.m., giving eight hours in bed. The short-night group went to bed at 2 a.m., and was woken at 6 a.m., giving four hours in bed. The no-sleep group stayed awake all night, in the laboratory, under supervision, and was not allowed to sleep, or to nap, or to drink coffee after midnight. All three groups were tested at 8 a.m., twelve hours after learning. The test had two parts. First, free recall: the participant wrote down as many of the forty words as could be remembered, in any order, in three minutes. Second, cued recall: the participant was given the first two letters of each word, in a random order, and was asked to complete the word, in three minutes. After the tests, each participant completed a questionnaire about their sleep, their alertness, and their confidence in their recall.

2.4 Analysis

Free recall and cued recall were scored as the number of words correctly recalled, out of forty. The data were analysed by one-way analysis of variance, with sleep condition as the between-participants factor, for free recall and for cued recall separately. Pairwise comparisons were made with the Tukey test. The relationship between baseline recall and test recall was examined by correlation, and the effect of age and of habitual sleep duration was examined by analysis of covariance. The level of significance was set at p < .05, and all tests were two-tailed.

3. Results

3.1 Baseline

Baseline free recall, measured immediately after learning, did not differ between the groups. The full-night group recalled a mean of 18.2 words, the short-night group 17.9, and the no-sleep group 18.4. Analysis of variance showed no significant difference, F(2, 87) = 0.21, p = .81. The groups were matched at learning, and any difference at test could be attributed to the sleep condition, not to a difference in learning.

3.2 Free recall

Free recall at test, twelve hours after learning, differed clearly between the groups. The full-night group recalled a mean of 24.6 words (standard deviation 4.1). The short-night group recalled a mean of 19.8 (standard deviation 4.6). The no-sleep group recalled a mean of 15.3 (standard deviation 4.9). Analysis of variance showed a significant main effect of sleep condition, F(2, 87) = 32.84, p < .001. All pairwise comparisons were significant: full-night better than short-night (p < .001), short-night better than no-sleep (p < .001), full-night better than no-sleep (p < .001). The difference between the full-night and the no-sleep group was 9.3 words, or 23 per cent of the list. The difference between the full-night and the short-night group was 4.8 words, and between the short-night and the no-sleep group 4.5 words. The decline was orderly: each halving of the sleep, from eight hours to four, and from four to none, cost about four to five words.

It is worth noting how the groups changed from baseline to test. The full-night group rose from 18.2 to 24.6 words, and the short-night group rose from 17.9 to 19.8. The no-sleep group fell, from 18.4 to 15.3. The improvement in the sleep groups is the consolidation effect: the memory strengthened during sleep, even without further study. The decline in the no-sleep group is the forgetting effect: the memory weakened, during twelve hours of waking, without sleep to protect it.

3.3 Cued recall

Cued recall showed the same pattern, at higher levels. The full-night group completed a mean of 31.2 words (standard deviation 3.8). The short-night group completed 27.4 (standard deviation 4.2). The no-sleep group completed 22.9 (standard deviation 4.7). Analysis of variance showed a significant main effect, F(2, 87) = 28.16, p < .001, and all pairwise comparisons were significant (all p < .001). The cue — the first two letters — helped all groups, by about six to seven words, but it did not remove the sleep effect. The full-night group was still 8.3 words ahead of the no-sleep group, even with the cue. The cue compensates for a weaker trace, but it does not replace the trace, and the trace is what sleep builds.

3.4 Other measures

Age had no significant effect on recall, F(1, 86) = 0.87, p = .35, and habitual sleep duration had no significant effect, F(1, 86) = 1.12, p = .29. Alertness, measured by the questionnaire, differed between the groups: the no-sleep group reported the lowest alertness, the full-night group the highest, and the short-night group in between. But alertness did not explain the recall difference: when alertness was controlled statistically, the effect of sleep condition on recall remained significant, F(2, 86) = 26.41, p < .001. The recall difference is not a matter of being sleepy at the test. It is a matter of what sleep did, during the night, to the memory.

3.5 Confidence

The questionnaire also asked participants how confident they were in their recall, on a scale from 1 (not at all confident) to 5 (very confident), before they saw their scores. The full-night group reported a mean confidence of 3.8 (standard deviation 0.7). The short-night group reported 3.2 (standard deviation 0.8). The no-sleep group reported 2.6 (standard deviation 0.9). Analysis of variance showed a significant main effect, F(2, 87) = 18.42, p < .001, and all pairwise comparisons were significant (all p < .01). The participants knew, in broad terms, how well they had done: the confidence scores followed the same order as the recall scores, and the correlation between confidence and free recall, across all participants, was r = .61, p < .001. But the confidence was not accurate in detail. The no-sleep group, which recalled 15.3 words out of 40, rated their confidence at 2.6 out of 5, which is just above the middle of the scale, and higher than their performance warranted. The full-night group, which recalled 24.6 words, rated their confidence at 3.8, which is below the top of the scale, and lower than their performance warranted. The sleep-deprived overestimated themselves, and the well-slept underestimated themselves, and the gap between confidence and performance was largest where the sleep was shortest. The finding is a warning: the person who has slept least is the person least able to judge how much has been lost, and the loss is therefore easy to miss, and easy to repeat.

4. Discussion

The study found a clear dose-response relationship between sleep duration and next-day recall. Eight hours of sleep gave the best recall, four hours gave less, and no sleep gave the least, and the decline was orderly: each halving of the sleep cost about four to five words, on a list of forty. The effect was present for free recall and for cued recall, and it was present after controlling for alertness, and for age, and for habitual sleep. The finding is simple, and it is important, because it puts a number on something that everyone knows in general: that sleep helps the memory, and that more sleep helps more.

The finding is consistent with the consolidation account. Sleep does not merely protect memory from interference. It actively strengthens it, and the strengthening depends on the amount of sleep. The full-night group did not merely forget less. They remembered more than they had at baseline — 24.6 words, against 18.2 immediately after learning. That is an improvement of 6.4 words, without further study, and it can only be explained by consolidation: by the brain working on the memory, during sleep, and making it stronger. The short-night group improved too, but less: from 17.9 to 19.8, an improvement of 1.9 words. The no-sleep group declined, from 18.4 to 15.3, a loss of 3.1 words. The pattern is the consolidation story, told in numbers: more sleep, more consolidation, more recall.

The cued-recall results add a second point. The cue helped all groups, by about six to seven words, but it did not remove the sleep effect. The full-night group was still 8.3 words ahead of the no-sleep group, even with the cue. This matters, because it shows that the sleep effect is not a matter of retrieval — of being able to find the word, when prompted. It is a matter of the trace itself: of how strongly the word is stored. A cue can help a weak trace to be found, but it cannot make a weak trace strong, and the trace is what sleep builds. The student who has slept, and the student who has not, will differ, even on a test that gives hints, because the hints cannot replace the consolidation.

The study has limits, and they should be stated plainly. The participants were young adults, aged eighteen to forty, and the results may not generalise to children, or to older adults, whose sleep is different, and whose memory is different. The material was a list of unrelated words, and the results may not generalise to connected material, such as a story, or an argument, or a skill, which may consolidate differently. The sleep was measured in hours in bed, not in stages, and the study cannot say which stages did the work, although the literature suggests that slow-wave sleep, in the first part of the night, is the most important for declarative memory, and the short-night group, which slept from 2 a.m. to 6 a.m., will have had less slow-wave sleep, and more rapid-eye-movement sleep, than the full-night group. The study also used a single night, and a single test, twelve hours after learning. The effect of chronic short sleep, over weeks, or of repeated testing, over days, is a question for further research.

The practical implications are straightforward, and they are worth stating plainly, because they are often ignored. A student who cuts sleep to study will remember less, not more, of what was studied. The hours spent awake, studying, are bought with the hours of sleep that would have consolidated the studying, and the bargain is a bad one. The study puts a number on the bargain: four hours of sleep, instead of eight, costs about five words in forty, or twelve per cent of the material. No sleep costs about nine words, or twenty-three per cent. These are not small losses, and they are losses that cannot be recovered by studying harder, because the loss is in consolidation, not in learning. The remedy is to sleep, and to sleep enough, and to treat sleep as a part of studying, not as its enemy.

The same applies to shift workers, and to anyone who must remember what was learned the day before. The worker who sleeps four hours, between shifts, will remember less of the training, and less of the instructions, than the worker who sleeps eight, and the difference will show in the work. The remedy is the same: protect the sleep, and the memory will protect itself.

5. Conclusion

Sleep duration determines next-day recall, in an orderly, dose-response relationship. Eight hours of sleep gives the best recall, four hours gives less, and no sleep gives the least, for both free recall and cued recall, and the difference is not explained by alertness, or by age, or by habitual sleep. Sleep consolidates memory, and the consolidation depends on the amount of sleep, and the loss from short sleep cannot be recovered by cues, or by effort, at the test. The practical conclusion is simple: to remember what was learned, sleep, and sleep enough. The night is not the enemy of the memory. It is its workshop, and the work it does there cannot be done anywhere else.

References

Diekelmann, S., and Born, J. "The Memory Function of Sleep." Nature Reviews Neuroscience 11 (2010), pp. 114-126.
Ebbinghaus, H. Über das Gedächtnis: Untersuchungen zur experimentellen Psychologie. Leipzig: Duncker & Humblot, 1885.
Jenkins, J. G., and Dallenbach, K. M. "Obliviscence during Sleep and Waking." American Journal of Psychology 35 (1924), pp. 605-612.
Walker, M. P., and Stickgold, R. "Sleep-Dependent Learning and Memory Consolidation." Neuron 44 (2004), pp. 121-133.
Walker, M. P. "A Refined Model of Sleep and the Time Course of Memory Formation." Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28 (2005), pp. 51-64.

His method, of learning to a criterion and testing after a delay, is the method used here, with real words instead of nonsense syllables, because real words are what people need to remember, in life, and the study was designed to be practical, as well as scientific.\n\nJenkins and Dallenbach, in 1924, made the first direct comparison of sleep and waking. They had participants learn nonsense syllables, and then either sleep or stay awake, for one, two, four, or eight hours, and then recall them. The sleepers forgot less, at every interval, and the difference grew with time. Their study is the ancestor of this one, and the present study repeats its design, with three changes: real words instead of nonsense syllables, a fixed twelve-hour delay, and three sleep durations, so that the dose-response curve can be mapped.\n\nThe modern consolidation literature adds the mechanism. Diekelmann and Born, in 2010, reviewed the evidence that sleep consolidates memory, and proposed that the consolidation is an active process, in which the hippocampus replays the day\'s learning during slow-wave sleep, and transfers it to the neocortex, for long-term storage. Walker, in 2005, and in later work, showed that sleep deprivation impairs the formation of new memories, as well as the retention of old ones, and that the impairment is proportional to the loss of sleep. The present study is consistent with this literature, and it tests a prediction that follows from it: that the amount of consolidation, and therefore the amount recalled, should depend on the amount of sleep, and should decline, in an orderly way, as sleep is shortened.\n\n2. Methods\n\n2.1 Participants\n\nNinety adults took part in the study, forty-five women and forty-five men, aged between eighteen and forty, with a mean age of twenty-six. All were native speakers of English, and all reported sleeping between seven and nine hours a night, habitually. None reported a sleep disorder, and none was taking medication that affected sleep. Participants were recruited from the local community, through notices in libraries and community centres, and were paid a small fee. Each participant attended two sessions: an evening learning session, and a morning test session, twelve hours later.\n\n2.2 Materials\n\nThe learning material was a list of forty unrelated English nouns, chosen to be concrete, familiar, and of similar frequency in the language. The words were: table, river, candle, garden, hammer, window, bridge, pillow, anchor, feather, kettle, valley, pocket, ladder, mirror, needle, saddle, basket, chimney, island, button, carpet, dagger, engine, forest, guitar, harbour, lantern, magnet, napkin, orchard, palace, quarry, ribbon, tunnel, temple, umbrella, village, wallet, yarn, and zebra. Each word was printed on a separate card, in large type, and the cards were presented in a fixed order, which was the same for all participants.\n\n2.3 Procedure\n\nThe learning session began at 8 p.m. Each participant was shown the forty cards, one at a time, for five seconds each, and was asked to read the word aloud, and to try to remember it. After all forty cards had been shown, the participant was given a five-minute break, and then was tested, by free recall, to establish a baseline: the participant wrote down as many of the forty words as could be remembered, in any order, in two minutes. The baseline was used to check that the groups were matched, and it was not counted in the results. After the baseline test, the participant was assigned to one of three sleep conditions, by random allocation, thirty participants to each condition.\n\nThe full-night group went to bed at 10 p.m., in the sleep laboratory, and was woken at 6 a.m., giving eight hours in bed. The short-night group went to bed at 2 a.m., and was woken at 6 a.m., giving four hours in bed. The no-sleep group stayed awake all night, in the laboratory, under supervision, and was not allowed to sleep, or to nap, or to drink coffee after midnight. All three groups were tested at 8 a.m., twelve hours after learning. The test had two parts. First, free recall: the participant wrote down as many of the forty words as could be remembered, in any order, in three minutes. Second, cued recall: the participant was given the first two letters of each word, in a random order, and was asked to complete the word, in three minutes. After the tests, each participant completed a questionnaire about their sleep, their alertness, and their confidence in their recall.\n\n2.4 Analysis\n\nFree recall and cued recall were scored as the number of words correctly recalled, out of forty. The data were analysed by one-way analysis of variance, with sleep condition as the between-participants factor, for free recall and for cued recall separately. Pairwise comparisons were made with the Tukey test. The relationship between baseline recall and test recall was examined by correlation, and the effect of age and of habitual sleep duration was examined by analysis of covariance. The level of significance was set at p < .05, and all tests were two-tailed.\n\n3. Results\n\n3.1 Baseline\n\nBaseline free recall, measured immediately after learning, did not differ between the groups. The full-night group recalled a mean of 18.2 words, the short-night group 17.9, and the no-sleep group 18.4. Analysis of variance showed no significant difference, F(2, 87) = 0.21, p = .81. The groups were matched at learning, and any difference at test could be attributed to the sleep condition, not to a difference in learning.\n\n3.2 Free recall\n\nFree recall at test, twelve hours after learning, differed clearly between the groups. The full-night group recalled a mean of 24.6 words (standard deviation 4.1). The short-night group recalled a mean of 19.8 (standard deviation 4.6). The no-sleep group recalled a mean of 15.3 (standard deviation 4.9). Analysis of variance showed a significant main effect of sleep condition, F(2, 87) = 32.84, p < .001. All pairwise comparisons were significant: full-night better than short-night (p < .001), short-night better than no-sleep (p < .001), full-night better than no-sleep (p < .001). The difference between the full-night and the no-sleep group was 9.3 words, or 23 per cent of the list. The difference between the full-night and the short-night group was 4.8 words, and between the short-night and the no-sleep group 4.5 words. The decline was orderly: each halving of the sleep, from eight hours to four, and from four to none, cost about four to five words.\n\nIt is worth noting how the groups changed from baseline to test. The full-night group rose from 18.2 to 24.6 words, and the short-night group rose from 17.9 to 19.8. The no-sleep group fell, from 18.4 to 15.3. The improvement in the sleep groups is the consolidation effect: the memory strengthened during sleep, even without further study. The decline in the no-sleep group is the forgetting effect: the memory weakened, during twelve hours of waking, without sleep to protect it.\n\n3.3 Cued recall\n\nCued recall showed the same pattern, at higher levels. The full-night group completed a mean of 31.2 words (standard deviation 3.8). The short-night group completed 27.4 (standard deviation 4.2). The no-sleep group completed 22.9 (standard deviation 4.7). Analysis of variance showed a significant main effect, F(2, 87) = 28.16, p < .001, and all pairwise comparisons were significant (all p < .001). The cue — the first two letters — helped all groups, by about six to seven words, but it did not remove the sleep effect. The full-night group was still 8.3 words ahead of the no-sleep group, even with the cue. The cue compensates for a weaker trace, but it does not replace the trace, and the trace is what sleep builds.\n\n3.4 Other measures\n\nAge had no significant effect on recall, F(1, 86) = 0.87, p = .35, and habitual sleep duration had no significant effect, F(1, 86) = 1.12, p = .29. Alertness, measured by the questionnaire, differed between the groups: the no-sleep group reported the lowest alertness, the full-night group the highest, and the short-night group in between. But alertness did not explain the recall difference: when alertness was controlled statistically, the effect of sleep condition on recall remained significant, F(2, 86) = 26.41, p < .001. The recall difference is not a matter of being sleepy at the test. It is a matter of what sleep did, during the night, to the memory.\n\n3.5 Confidence\n\nThe questionnaire also asked participants how confident they were in their recall, on a scale from 1 (not at all confident) to 5 (very confident), before they saw their scores. The full-night group reported a mean confidence of 3.8 (standard deviation 0.7). The short-night group reported 3.2 (standard deviation 0.8). The no-sleep group reported 2.6 (standard deviation 0.9). Analysis of variance showed a significant main effect, F(2, 87) = 18.42, p < .001, and all pairwise comparisons were significant (all p < .01). The participants knew, in broad terms, how well they had done: the confidence scores followed the same order as the recall scores, and the correlation between confidence and free recall, across all participants, was r = .61, p < .001. But the confidence was not accurate in detail. The no-sleep group, which recalled 15.3 words out of 40, rated their confidence at 2.6 out of 5, which is just above the middle of the scale, and higher than their performance warranted. The full-night group, which recalled 24.6 words, rated their confidence at 3.8, which is below the top of the scale, and lower than their performance warranted. The sleep-deprived overestimated themselves, and the well-slept underestimated themselves, and the gap between confidence and performance was largest where the sleep was shortest. The finding is a warning: the person who has slept least is the person least able to judge how much has been lost, and the loss is therefore easy to miss, and easy to repeat.\n\n4. Discussion\n\nThe study found a clear dose-response relationship between sleep duration and next-day recall. Eight hours of sleep gave the best recall, four hours gave less, and no sleep gave the least, and the decline was orderly: each halving of the sleep cost about four to five words, on a list of forty. The effect was present for free recall and for cued recall, and it was present after controlling for alertness, and for age, and for habitual sleep. The finding is simple, and it is important, because it puts a number on something that everyone knows in general: that sleep helps the memory, and that more sleep helps more.\n\nThe finding is consistent with the consolidation account. Sleep does not merely protect memory from interference. It actively strengthens it, and the strengthening depends on the amount of sleep. The full-night group did not merely forget less. They remembered more than they had at baseline — 24.6 words, against 18.2 immediately after learning. That is an improvement of 6.4 words, without further study, and it can only be explained by consolidation: by the brain working on the memory, during sleep, and making it stronger. The short-night group improved too, but less: from 17.9 to 19.8, an improvement of 1.9 words. The no-sleep group declined, from 18.4 to 15.3, a loss of 3.1 words. The pattern is the consolidation story, told in numbers: more sleep, more consolidation, more recall.\n\nThe cued-recall results add a second point. The cue helped all groups, by about six to seven words, but it did not remove the sleep effect. The full-night group was still 8.3 words ahead of the no-sleep group, even with the cue. This matters, because it shows that the sleep effect is not a matter of retrieval — of being able to find the word, when prompted. It is a matter of the trace itself: of how strongly the word is stored. A cue can help a weak trace to be found, but it cannot make a weak trace strong, and the trace is what sleep builds. The student who has slept, and the student who has not, will differ, even on a test that gives hints, because the hints cannot replace the consolidation.\n\nThe study has limits, and they should be stated plainly. The participants were young adults, aged eighteen to forty, and the results may not generalise to children, or to older adults, whose sleep is different, and whose memory is different. The material was a list of unrelated words, and the results may not generalise to connected material, such as a story, or an argument, or a skill, which may consolidate differently. The sleep was measured in hours in bed, not in stages, and the study cannot say which stages did the work, although the literature suggests that slow-wave sleep, in the first part of the night, is the most important for declarative memory, and the short-night group, which slept from 2 a.m. to 6 a.m., will have had less slow-wave sleep, and more rapid-eye-movement sleep, than the full-night group. The study also used a single night, and a single test, twelve hours after learning. The effect of chronic short sleep, over weeks, or of repeated testing, over days, is a question for further research.\n\nThe practical implications are straightforward, and they are worth stating plainly, because they are often ignored. A student who cuts sleep to study will remember less, not more, of what was studied. The hours spent awake, studying, are bought with the hours of sleep that would have consolidated the studying, and the bargain is a bad one. The study puts a number on the bargain: four hours of sleep, instead of eight, costs about five words in forty, or twelve per cent of the material. No sleep costs about nine words, or twenty-three per cent. These are not small losses, and they are losses that cannot be recovered by studying harder, because the loss is in consolidation, not in learning. The remedy is to sleep, and to sleep enough, and to treat sleep as a part of studying, not as its enemy.\n\nThe same applies to shift workers, and to anyone who must remember what was learned the day before. The worker who sleeps four hours, between shifts, will remember less of the training, and less of the instructions, than the worker who sleeps eight, and the difference will show in the work. The remedy is the same: protect the sleep, and the memory will protect itself.\n\n5. Conclusion\n\nSleep duration determines next-day recall, in an orderly, dose-response relationship. Eight hours of sleep gives the best recall, four hours gives less, and no sleep gives the least, for both free recall and cued recall, and the difference is not explained by alertness, or by age, or by habitual sleep. Sleep consolidates memory, and the consolidation depends on the amount of sleep, and the loss from short sleep cannot be recovered by cues, or by effort, at the test. It is its workshop, and the work it does there cannot be done anywhere else.\n\nReferences\n\nDiekelmann, S., and Born, J. "The Memory Function of Sleep." Nature Reviews Neuroscience 11 (2010), pp. 114-126.\nEbbinghaus, H. Über das Gedächtnis: Untersuchungen zur experimentellen Psychologie. Leipzig: Duncker & Humblot, 1885.\nJenkins, J. G., and Dallenbach, K. M. "Obliviscence during Sleep and Waking." American Journal of Psychology 35 (1924), pp. 605-612.\nWalker, M. P., and Stickgold, R. "Sleep-Dependent Learning and Memory Consolidation." Neuron 44 (2004), pp. 121-133.\nWalker, M. P. "A Refined Model of Sleep and the Time Course of Memory Formation." Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28 (2005), pp. 51-64.\n'
TITLE = 'Sleep Duration and Next-Day Recall of Word Lists: An Experimental Study'
words = TEXT.split()
wc = len(words)
sc = len(re.findall(r"[.!?]+[\"')\]]*\s", TEXT + " ")) + (1 if re.search(r"[.!?][\"')\]]*\s*$", TEXT.strip()) else 0)
pc = len([p for p in TEXT.split("\n\n") if p.strip()])
rt = -(-wc // 200)
avg = wc / sc if sc else 0
uniq = len({w.strip(".,;:!?\"'()[]").lower() for w in words if w.strip(".,;:!?\"'()[]")})
toks = [w.strip(".,;:!?\"'()[]").lower() for w in words]
stop = set("a an the and or of to in on for with as at by from is was are were be been being it its this that these those he she they we you i his her their our your my me him us them not no but so if then than when while who whom which what how all any some more most other into over under out up down off about after before between through during against without within upon per via".split())
toks = [t for t in toks if len(t) > 3 and t.isalpha() and t not in stop]
top = Counter(toks).most_common(5)
longest = max((w.strip(".,;:!?\"'()[]") for w in words), key=len, default="")
print(f"Title: {TITLE}")
print(f"Words: {wc}")
print(f"Sentences: {sc}")
print(f"Paragraphs: {pc}")
print(f"Reading time at 200 words per minute: {wc} / 200 = {wc / 200:.2f}, rounded up = {rt} minutes")
print(f"Average sentence length: {wc} / {sc} = {avg:.1f} words" if sc else "Average sentence length: no sentences found")
print(f"Unique words: {uniq}")
print(f"Longest word: {longest} ({len(longest)} letters)")
print("Most frequent words (over 3 letters): " + ", ".join(f"{w} ({c})" for w, c in top))

The no-sleep group, which recalled 15.3 words out of 40, rated their confidence at 2.6 out of 5, which is just above the middle of the scale, and higher than their performance warranted. The full-night group, which recalled 24.6 words, rated their confidence at 3.8, which is below the top of the scale, and lower than their performance warranted. The sleep-deprived overestimated themselves, and the well-slept underestimated themselves, and the gap between confidence and performance was largest where the sleep was shortest. The finding is a warning: the person who has slept least is the person least able to judge how much has been lost, and the loss is therefore easy to miss, and easy to repeat.\n\n4. Discussion\n\nThe study found a clear dose-response relationship between sleep duration and next-day recall. Eight hours of sleep gave the best recall, four hours gave less, and no sleep gave the least, and the decline was orderly: each halving of the sleep cost about four to five words, on a list of forty. The effect was present for free recall and for cued recall, and it was present after controlling for alertness, and for age, and for habitual sleep. The finding is simple, and it is important, because it puts a number on something that everyone knows in general: that sleep helps the memory, and that more sleep helps more.\n\nThe finding is consistent with the consolidation account. Sleep does not merely protect memory from interference. It actively strengthens it, and the strengthening depends on the amount of sleep. The full-night group did not merely forget less. They remembered more than they had at baseline — 24.6 words, against 18.2 immediately after learning. That is an improvement of 6.4 words, without further study, and it can only be explained by consolidation: by the brain working on the memory, during sleep, and making it stronger. The short-night group improved too, but less: from 17.9 to 19.8, an improvement of 1.9 words. The no-sleep group declined, from 18.4 to 15.3, a loss of 3.1 words. The pattern is the consolidation story, told in numbers: more sleep, more consolidation, more recall.\n\nThe cued-recall results add a second point. The cue helped all groups, by about six to seven words, but it did not remove the sleep effect. The full-night group was still 8.3 words ahead of the no-sleep group, even with the cue. This matters, because it shows that the sleep effect is not a matter of retrieval — of being able to find the word, when prompted. It is a matter of the trace itself: of how strongly the word is stored. A cue can help a weak trace to be found, but it cannot make a weak trace strong, and the trace is what sleep builds. The student who has slept, and the student who has not, will differ, even on a test that gives hints, because the hints cannot replace the consolidation.\n\nThe study has limits, and they should be stated plainly. The participants were young adults, aged eighteen to forty, and the results may not generalise to children, or to older adults, whose sleep is different, and whose memory is different. The material was a list of unrelated words, and the results may not generalise to connected material, such as a story, or an argument, or a skill, which may consolidate differently. The sleep was measured in hours in bed, not in stages, and the study cannot say which stages did the work, although the literature suggests that slow-wave sleep, in the first part of the night, is the most important for declarative memory, and the short-night group, which slept from 2 a.m. to 6 a.m., will have had less slow-wave sleep, and more rapid-eye-movement sleep, than the full-night group. The study also used a single night, and a single test, twelve hours after learning. The effect of chronic short sleep, over weeks, or of repeated testing, over days, is a question for further research.\n\nThe practical implications are straightforward, and they are worth stating plainly, because they are often ignored. A student who cuts sleep to study will remember less, not more, of what was studied. The hours spent awake, studying, are bought with the hours of sleep that would have consolidated the studying, and the bargain is a bad one. The study puts a number on the bargain: four hours of sleep, instead of eight, costs about five words in forty, or twelve per cent of the material. No sleep costs about nine words, or twenty-three per cent. These are not small losses, and they are losses that cannot be recovered by studying harder, because the loss is in consolidation, not in learning. The remedy is to sleep, and to sleep enough, and to treat sleep as a part of studying, not as its enemy.\n\nThe same applies to shift workers, and to anyone who must remember what was learned the day before. The worker who sleeps four hours, between shifts, will remember less of the training, and less of the instructions, than the worker who sleeps eight, and the difference will show in the work. The remedy is the same: protect the sleep, and the memory will protect itself.\n\n5. Conclusion\n\nSleep duration determines next-day recall, in an orderly, dose-response relationship. Eight hours of sleep gives the best recall, four hours gives less, and no sleep gives the least, for both free recall and cued recall, and the difference is not explained by alertness, or by age, or by habitual sleep. Sleep consolidates memory, and the consolidation depends on the amount of sleep, and the loss from short sleep cannot be recovered by cues, or by effort, at the test. The practical conclusion is simple: to remember what was learned, sleep, and sleep enough. The night is not the enemy of the memory. It is its workshop, and the work it does there cannot be done anywhere else.\n\nReferences\n\nDiekelmann, S., and Born, J. "The Memory Function of Sleep." Nature Reviews Neuroscience 11 (2010), pp. 114-126.\nEbbinghaus, H. Über das Gedächtnis: Untersuchungen zur experimentellen Psychologie. Leipzig: Duncker & Humblot, 1885.\nJenkins, J. Full text

PUBLIC LIBRARY USE IN SMALL TOWNS: A SURVEY OF TWELVE LIBRARIES

Abstract

This study surveyed the use of public libraries in twelve small towns, each with a population between 2,000 and 10,000, over a period of six months. Six hundred library users were interviewed, and the libraries' records were examined, to answer three questions: who uses the small-town library, what do they use it for, and what would they lose if it closed? The results show that the library is used by all ages, but most heavily by children and by older adults; that borrowing books remains the most common use, but that the library is also used as a meeting place, as a source of help with forms and with technology, and as a warm, quiet room; and that the loss of the library would be felt most by those with the fewest alternatives. The findings support the view that the small-town library is a public good, and that its value cannot be measured by borrowing figures alone.

1. Introduction

The public library is one of the oldest public institutions, and one of the least questioned. It is also one of the least measured. The borrowing figures are counted, and the visits are counted, and the budgets are counted, but the use — what people actually do in the library, and what it means to them — is rarely studied, and more rarely in small towns, where the library is often the only public room in the place, and where its closing would leave a hole that nothing else would fill. This study is an attempt to measure that use, in twelve small towns, over six months, by asking the users themselves.

The small town is a particular case. In a city, the library is one institution among many: there are other rooms, other books, other places to meet, other sources of help. In a small town, the library is often the only one. It is the only place with books to borrow, the only place with a computer to use, the only place with someone to ask, the only warm room that is free, and open to all, without a purchase, and without a purpose. The small-town library is therefore a test of the public library idea, in its purest form: a place that exists for the public, and for no other reason, and that serves whoever walks in, for whatever they need.

The study was designed to answer three questions. First, who uses the small-town library? The answer is not obvious. The library is open to all, but not all use it, and the pattern of use — by age, by occupation, by frequency — tells us who the library serves, and who it does not. Second, what do they use it for? Borrowing books is the obvious answer, but it is not the only one, and the other uses — meeting, asking, sitting, keeping warm, using the computer, attending the children's hour — may matter as much as the borrowing, or more. Third, what would they lose if it closed? The answer to that question is the measure of the library's value, and it cannot be found in the borrowing figures, because the borrowing figures count only the books, and the library is more than the books.

The study's hypothesis was that the library would be used by all ages, but most by the young and the old; that borrowing would be the most common use, but not the only one; and that the loss, if the library closed, would be felt most by those with the least money, and the fewest alternatives. The study was designed to test these hypotheses, and to give the libraries, and the towns, a picture of what they have, and what they would lose.

1.1 Previous research

The public library has been written about since its founding, but the writing has been more often advocacy than research. Ranganathan, in 1931, set out the five laws of library science — books are for use, every reader his book, every book its reader, save the time of the reader, the library is a growing organism — and the laws have guided librarians ever since, because they state the library's purpose in a sentence, and the purpose is the use. Carnegie, in 1889, argued that the rich man should give his wealth to the public, and that the public library was the best gift, because it gave the poor man the means to educate himself, and the gift was not a dole, but a tool. The libraries that Carnegie founded, all over the English-speaking world, are the ancestors of the libraries in this study, and the study is, in a sense, a test of Carnegie's argument, a hundred and thirty years later.

Shera, in 1949, wrote the history of the public library, and showed that it grew out of two ideas: the idea that knowledge should be free, and the idea that the public should pay for it. The American Library Association, in its annual State of America's Libraries reports, has documented the library's use, year by year, and has shown that the use persists, and grows, even as the forms change: the books are borrowed, and the computers are used, and the programs are attended, and the library remains, in the Association's phrase, the heart of the community. The present study builds on this literature, and it adds to it in one respect: it studies the small town, where the library's role is largest, and where it has been studied least.

2. Methods

2.1 Libraries

Twelve libraries took part in the study, in twelve small towns, in three counties. The towns had populations between 2,000 and 10,000, with a mean of 5,400. Each town had one public library, open at least thirty hours a week, with at least one full-time librarian. The libraries were chosen to vary in size, in opening hours, and in the range of services offered, so that the study could compare them. Four of the libraries were in towns with a population under 3,000, four in towns of 3,000 to 6,000, and four in towns of 6,000 to 10,000. The libraries' records — borrowing figures, visit counts, program attendance — were examined for the six months of the study, and for the six months before it, for comparison.

2.2 Participants

Six hundred library users were interviewed, fifty from each library. The users were approached in the library, at different times of day, and on different days of the week, and were asked to take part in a short interview, lasting about ten minutes. The interview was voluntary, and anonymous, and the users were told that their answers would be used for research, and would not be traced to them. Of those approached, 612 were asked, and 600 agreed, a response rate of 98 per cent. The sample included 342 women and 258 men, aged from 7 to 89, with a mean age of 41. The sample was not a sample of the town's population. It was a sample of the library's users, and the study's questions are about the users, not about the town.

2.3 Interview

The interview had three parts. The first part asked who the user was: age, occupation, how often the user visited the library, and how long the user had been using it. The second part asked what the user did in the library: borrowing books, reading newspapers, using the computer, attending programs, meeting people, asking for help, sitting and reading, keeping warm, and any other use the user named. The user was asked to name all the uses, and to say which was the most important. The third part asked what the user would lose if the library closed: the user was asked to imagine the library closed, and to say what would be lost, and what would be done instead, and whether there was anywhere else to go for the same purpose. The interviews were conducted by the researcher, and by two assistants, and were recorded in writing, on a standard form, at the time of the interview.

2.4 Analysis

The interview data were counted, and the counts were expressed as percentages, and as numbers, and were compared across libraries, and across age groups, and across frequency of use. The libraries' records were used to check the interview data, and to give the context: the borrowing figures, the visit counts, and the program attendance, for the six months of the study. The analysis was descriptive, and the study does not claim to prove causation. It describes the use, and it reports what the users said, and it draws conclusions from the pattern, not from a test.

3. Results

3.1 Who uses the library

The users were of all ages, but the distribution was not even. Children under twelve made up 18 per cent of the users interviewed. Young people, aged thirteen to twenty-five, made up 14 per cent. Adults, aged twenty-six to sixty-five, made up 44 per cent. Older adults, over sixty-five, made up 24 per cent. The library is used most by adults, but the young and the old are over-represented, compared with their share of the town's population, and the middle-aged are under-represented. The pattern is consistent with the library's role: the young use it because they have time, and the old use it because they have time, and the middle-aged, who are working, use it less, because they have less time.

Frequency of use varied. Thirty-two per cent of users visited at least once a week. Twenty-eight per cent visited once a fortnight. Twenty-two per cent visited once a month. Eighteen per cent visited less often. The frequent users — those who visited at least once a week — were disproportionately children and older adults. The infrequent users were disproportionately adults of working age. Length of use also varied: 41 per cent of users had been using the library for more than ten years, 29 per cent for between two and ten years, and 30 per cent for less than two years. The library has a core of long-term users, and a steady flow of new ones.

3.2 What they use it for

Borrowing books was the most common use, named by 78 per cent of users, and named as the most important use by 52 per cent. Reading newspapers and magazines in the library was named by 41 per cent. Using the computer was named by 38 per cent. Attending programs — the children's hour, the reading group, the talks — was named by 29 per cent. Meeting people was named by 24 per cent. Asking for help — with forms, with letters, with the computer, with finding information — was named by 22 per cent. Sitting and reading, without borrowing, was named by 19 per cent. Keeping warm was named by 11 per cent, all of them older adults, and all of them in the winter months. The uses overlap: the average user named 2.6 uses, and only 18 per cent named borrowing alone.

The uses varied by age. Children named borrowing, and programs, and meeting friends. Young people named the computer, and borrowing, and studying. Adults named borrowing, and the computer, and asking for help. Older adults named borrowing, and reading newspapers, and meeting people, and keeping warm. The library serves different purposes for different ages, and the purposes change with the stage of life, and the library's strength is that it serves them all, in the same room, at the same time.

3.3 What would be lost

When asked what would be lost if the library closed, 64 per cent of users said they would lose the books, and would have nowhere else to borrow them. Forty-one per cent said they would lose the computer, and would have nowhere else to use one. Thirty-three per cent said they would lose the meeting place, and would have nowhere else to meet. Twenty-seven per cent said they would lose the help, and would have nowhere else to ask. Nineteen per cent said they would lose the warm room, and would have nowhere else to go in the winter. Twelve per cent said they would lose nothing, because they could buy books, or use the internet at home, or go elsewhere. The twelve per cent were disproportionately the better-off users, with cars, and with computers at home. The users who would lose most were the poorest, and the oldest, and the youngest, and those without transport.

The libraries' records supported the interviews. Borrowing, over the six months, averaged 1,240 loans per library per month, or about 15,000 loans a year, for a town of 5,400 people — about three loans per person per year, for the whole town, and about twenty-five loans per user per year, for the users. Visits averaged 2,800 per library per month. Program attendance averaged 320 per library per month. The figures are modest, in absolute terms, and they are the figures that are used to judge the library, and they do not capture the meeting, and the help, and the warmth, which the users named, and which the figures cannot count.

3.4 The librarian

The interviews also asked about the librarian, and the answers were the warmest in the study. Seventy-one per cent of users said they had asked the librarian for help, at some time, and 58 per cent said they had asked in the last month. The help asked for was of many kinds: finding a book, 44 per cent; using the computer, 31 per cent; filling in a form, 18 per cent; finding information, 22 per cent; and other help, 12 per cent, including writing a letter, reading a letter, and making a telephone call. When asked what the librarian's help was worth, 83 per cent said it was very important, 12 per cent said it was fairly important, and 5 per cent said it was not important. The users who said it was very important were disproportionately the older users, and the users without a computer at home, and the users who had been using the library longest.

The users were also asked what would happen if the librarian were replaced by a machine — by a self-service kiosk, for borrowing, and by a computer, for information. Sixty-eight per cent said the library would be worse, and 21 per cent said it would be much worse. Only 4 per cent said it would be better, and 7 per cent said it would make no difference. The reasons given were consistent: the machine cannot answer a question that the user does not know how to ask, the machine cannot tell the user about a book the user has not thought of, and the machine cannot be kind. The librarian can do all three, and the doing is the service. The library, the users said, is not the books. It is the person who knows the books, and who knows the users, and who puts the two together. The finding is the study's most human result, and it is the one that the borrowing figures will never show.

4. Discussion

The study found what it expected to find, and it found more. The library is used by all ages, but most by the young and the old. Borrowing is the most common use, but it is not the only one, and the other uses — meeting, asking, sitting, keeping warm — are named by a quarter to a third of users, and are named as the most important use by a substantial minority. The loss, if the library closed, would fall hardest on those with the least: the poor, the old, the young, and those without transport. The library is a public good, and its value cannot be measured by borrowing figures alone, because the borrowing figures count only the books, and the library is more than the books.

The finding that the average user named 2.6 uses is the study's most important result. It shows that the library is not a single service, but a bundle of services, and that the bundle is the point. A user who borrows books, and uses the computer, and meets a friend, is using the library in three ways, and the three ways support each other: the friend tells the user about a book, the book leads the user to the computer, the computer leads the user to a form, the form is filled in with the librarian's help. The library is a place where uses combine, and the combination is the value. A library that only lent books would be a smaller thing, and a less valuable thing, than the library that lends books, and gives help, and gives warmth, and gives company, in the same room.

The finding that 11 per cent of users named keeping warm, all of them older adults, in the winter, deserves attention. It is a small figure, and it is a human figure. An older person, living alone, in a cold house, comes to the library to be warm, and to be among people, and the library gives both, without asking, and without charging. The borrowing figures will never show this. The visit counts will show that the person came, but not why. The interview shows why, and the why is the library's purpose, stated in Ranganathan's first law: books are for use, and the library is for use, and the use includes being warm, and being among people, and being welcome. A library that is judged only by its loans will be judged wrongly, and a library that is closed because its loans are low will have taken warmth, and company, and help, away from people who have nowhere else to go.

The study has limits, and they should be stated plainly. The sample was a sample of users, not of the town, and the study cannot say what proportion of the town uses the library, or why the rest do not. The interviews were short, and the answers were the users' own words, and the users may have overstated their use, or understated it, or given the answer they thought the interviewer wanted. The study covered six months, and the winter months will have raised the figure for keeping warm, and lowered the figure for other uses. The study covered twelve libraries, in three counties, and the libraries may not represent all small-town libraries, in all places. These limits do not invalidate the findings. They qualify them, and they point to further research: a study of non-users, a study over a full year, a study of more libraries, in more places.

The practical implications are for the towns, and for those who fund the libraries. The library should be judged by its uses, not only by its loans. The uses should be counted, and the counting should include the meeting, and the help, and the warmth, and the computer, and the programs, and the sitting, and the reading, and the borrowing, all together, because the together is the library. The library should be kept open, in the winter, and in the evenings, and at the weekends, because the users who need it most are the ones who come when it is cold, and when they are free, and the hours are the service. And the library should be staffed, by a librarian who knows the users, and who can help, because the help is the service that no machine can give, and the librarian is the reason the library is more than a room full of books.

5. Conclusion

The small-town library is used by all ages, for many purposes, and its loss would fall hardest on those with the least. Borrowing books is the most common use, but it is one use among many, and the library's value lies in the bundle: the books, and the computer, and the help, and the meeting, and the warmth, and the welcome. The borrowing figures do not capture the value, and the library should not be judged by them alone. The library is a public good, and its goodness is in its use, and its use is in the lives of the people who walk through its door, and who find, inside, what they cannot find anywhere else in the town.

References

American Library Association. State of America's Libraries Report. Chicago: American Library Association, 2023.
Carnegie, A. "The Gospel of Wealth." North American Review 148 (1889), pp. 653-664.
Ranganathan, S. R. The Five Laws of Library Science. Madras: Madras Library Association, 1931.
Shera, J. H. Foundations of the Public Library: The Origins of the Public Library Movement in New England, 1629-1855. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1949.
