The borrowing figures are counted, and the visits are counted, and the budgets are counted, but the use — what people actually do in the library, and what it means to them — is rarely studied, and more rarely in small towns, where the library is often the only public room in the place, and where its closing would leave a hole that nothing else would fill. This study is an attempt to measure that use, in twelve small towns, over six months, by asking the users themselves.\n\nThe small town is a particular case. In a city, the library is one institution among many: there are other rooms, other books, other places to meet, other sources of help. In a small town, the library is often the only one. It is the only place with books to borrow, the only place with a computer to use, the only place with someone to ask, the only warm room that is free, and open to all, without a purchase, and without a purpose. The small-town library is therefore a test of the public library idea, in its purest form: a place that exists for the public, and for no other reason, and that serves whoever walks in, for whatever they need.\n\nThe study was designed to answer three questions. First, who uses the small-town library? The answer is not obvious. The library is open to all, but not all use it, and the pattern of use — by age, by occupation, by frequency — tells us who the library serves, and who it does not. Second, what do they use it for? Borrowing books is the obvious answer, but it is not the only one, and the other uses — meeting, asking, sitting, keeping warm, using the computer, attending the children\'s hour — may matter as much as the borrowing, or more. Third, what would they lose if it closed? The answer to that question is the measure of the library\'s value, and it cannot be found in the borrowing figures, because the borrowing figures count only the books, and the library is more than the books.\n\nThe study\'s hypothesis was that the library would be used by all ages, but most by the young and the old; that borrowing would be the most common use, but not the only one; and that the loss, if the library closed, would be felt most by those with the least money, and the fewest alternatives. The study was designed to test these hypotheses, and to give the libraries, and the towns, a picture of what they have, and what they would lose.\n\n1.1 Previous research\n\nThe public library has been written about since its founding, but the writing has been more often advocacy than research. Ranganathan, in 1931, set out the five laws of library science — books are for use, every reader his book, every book its reader, save the time of the reader, the library is a growing organism — and the laws have guided librarians ever since, because they state the library\'s purpose in a sentence, and the purpose is the use. Carnegie, in 1889, argued that the rich man should give his wealth to the public, and that the public library was the best gift, because it gave the poor man the means to educate himself, and the gift was not a dole, but a tool. The libraries that Carnegie founded, all over the English-speaking world, are the ancestors of the libraries in this study, and the study is, in a sense, a test of Carnegie\'s argument, a hundred and thirty years later.\n\nShera, in 1949, wrote the history of the public library, and showed that it grew out of two ideas: the idea that knowledge should be free, and the idea that the public should pay for it. The American Library Association, in its annual State of America\'s Libraries reports, has documented the library\'s use, year by year, and has shown that the use persists, and grows, even as the forms change: the books are borrowed, and the computers are used, and the programs are attended, and the library remains, in the Association\'s phrase, the heart of the community. The present study builds on this literature, and it adds to it in one respect: it studies the small town, where the library\'s role is largest, and where it has been studied least.\n\n2. Methods\n\n2.1 Libraries\n\nTwelve libraries took part in the study, in twelve small towns, in three counties. The towns had populations between 2,000 and 10,000, with a mean of 5,400. Each town had one public library, open at least thirty hours a week, with at least one full-time librarian. The libraries were chosen to vary in size, in opening hours, and in the range of services offered, so that the study could compare them. Four of the libraries were in towns with a population under 3,000, four in towns of 3,000 to 6,000, and four in towns of 6,000 to 10,000. The libraries\' records — borrowing figures, visit counts, program attendance — were examined for the six months of the study, and for the six months before it, for comparison.\n\n2.2 Participants\n\nSix hundred library users were interviewed, fifty from each library. The users were approached in the library, at different times of day, and on different days of the week, and were asked to take part in a short interview, lasting about ten minutes. The interview was voluntary, and anonymous, and the users were told that their answers would be used for research, and would not be traced to them. Of those approached, 612 were asked, and 600 agreed, a response rate of 98 per cent. The sample included 342 women and 258 men, aged from 7 to 89, with a mean age of 41. The sample was not a sample of the town\'s population. It was a sample of the library\'s users, and the study\'s questions are about the users, not about the town.\n\n2.3 Interview\n\nThe interview had three parts. The first part asked who the user was: age, occupation, how often the user visited the library, and how long the user had been using it. The second part asked what the user did in the library: borrowing books, reading newspapers, using the computer, attending programs, meeting people, asking for help, sitting and reading, keeping warm, and any other use the user named. The user was asked to name all the uses, and to say which was the most important. The third part asked what the user would lose if the library closed: the user was asked to imagine the library closed, and to say what would be lost, and what would be done instead, and whether there was anywhere else to go for the same purpose. The interviews were conducted by the researcher, and by two assistants, and were recorded in writing, on a standard form, at the time of the interview.\n\n2.4 Analysis\n\nThe interview data were counted, and the counts were expressed as percentages, and as numbers, and were compared across libraries, and across age groups, and across frequency of use. The libraries\' records were used to check the interview data, and to give the context: the borrowing figures, the visit counts, and the program attendance, for the six months of the study. The analysis was descriptive, and the study does not claim to prove causation. It describes the use, and it reports what the users said, and it draws conclusions from the pattern, not from a test.\n\n3. Results\n\n3.1 Who uses the library\n\nThe users were of all ages, but the distribution was not even. Children under twelve made up 18 per cent of the users interviewed. Young people, aged thirteen to twenty-five, made up 14 per cent. Adults, aged twenty-six to sixty-five, made up 44 per cent. Older adults, over sixty-five, made up 24 per cent. The library is used most by adults, but the young and the old are over-represented, compared with their share of the town\'s population, and the middle-aged are under-represented. The pattern is consistent with the library\'s role: the young use it because they have time, and the old use it because they have time, and the middle-aged, who are working, use it less, because they have less time.\n\nFrequency of use varied. Thirty-two per cent of users visited at least once a week. Twenty-eight per cent visited once a fortnight. Twenty-two per cent visited once a month. Eighteen per cent visited less often. The frequent users — those who visited at least once a week — were disproportionately children and older adults. The infrequent users were disproportionately adults of working age. Length of use also varied: 41 per cent of users had been using the library for more than ten years, 29 per cent for between two and ten years, and 30 per cent for less than two years. The library has a core of long-term users, and a steady flow of new ones.\n\n3.2 What they use it for\n\nBorrowing books was the most common use, named by 78 per cent of users, and named as the most important use by 52 per cent. Reading newspapers and magazines in the library was named by 41 per cent. Using the computer was named by 38 per cent. Attending programs — the children\'s hour, the reading group, the talks — was named by 29 per cent. Meeting people was named by 24 per cent. Asking for help — with forms, with letters, with the computer, with finding information — was named by 22 per cent. Sitting and reading, without borrowing, was named by 19 per cent. Keeping warm was named by 11 per cent, all of them older adults, and all of them in the winter months. The uses overlap: the average user named 2.6 uses, and only 18 per cent named borrowing alone.\n\nThe uses varied by age. Children named borrowing, and programs, and meeting friends. Young people named the computer, and borrowing, and studying. Adults named borrowing, and the computer, and asking for help. Older adults named borrowing, and reading newspapers, and meeting people, and keeping warm. The library serves different purposes for different ages, and the purposes change with the stage of life, and the library\'s strength is that it serves them all, in the same room, at the same time.\n\n3.3 What would be lost\n\nWhen asked what would be lost if the library closed, 64 per cent of users said they would lose the books, and would have nowhere else to borrow them. Forty-one per cent said they would lose the computer, and would have nowhere else to use one. Thirty-three per cent said they would lose the meeting place, and would have nowhere else to meet. Twenty-seven per cent said they would lose the help, and would have nowhere else to ask. Nineteen per cent said they would lose the warm room, and would have nowhere else to go in the winter. Twelve per cent said they would lose nothing, because they could buy books, or use the internet at home, or go elsewhere. The twelve per cent were disproportionately the better-off users, with cars, and with computers at home. The users who would lose most were the poorest, and the oldest, and the youngest, and those without transport.\n\nThe libraries\' records supported the interviews. Borrowing, over the six months, averaged 1,240 loans per library per month, or about 15,000 loans a year, for a town of 5,400 people — about three loans per person per year, for the whole town, and about twenty-five loans per user per year, for the users. Visits averaged 2,800 per library per month. Program attendance averaged 320 per library per month. The figures are modest, in absolute terms, and they are the figures that are used to judge the library, and they do not capture the meeting, and the help, and the warmth, which the users named, and which the figures cannot count.\n\n3.4 The librarian\n\nThe interviews also asked about the librarian, and the answers were the warmest in the study. Seventy-one per cent of users said they had asked the librarian for help, at some time, and 58 per cent said they had asked in the last month. The help asked for was of many kinds: finding a book, 44 per cent; using the computer, 31 per cent; filling in a form, 18 per cent; finding information, 22 per cent; and other help, 12 per cent, including writing a letter, reading a letter, and making a telephone call. When asked what the librarian\'s help was worth, 83 per cent said it was very important, 12 per cent said it was fairly important, and 5 per cent said it was not important. The users who said it was very important were disproportionately the older users, and the users without a computer at home, and the users who had been using the library longest.\n\nThe users were also asked what would happen if the librarian were replaced by a machine — by a self-service kiosk, for borrowing, and by a computer, for information. Sixty-eight per cent said the library would be worse, and 21 per cent said it would be much worse. Only 4 per cent said it would be better, and 7 per cent said it would make no difference. The reasons given were consistent: the machine cannot answer a question that the user does not know how to ask, the machine cannot tell the user about a book the user has not thought of, and the machine cannot be kind. The librarian can do all three, and the doing is the service. The library, the users said, is not the books. It is the person who knows the books, and who knows the users, and who puts the two together. The finding is the study\'s most human result, and it is the one that the borrowing figures will never show.\n\n4. Discussion\n\nThe study found what it expected to find, and it found more. The library is used by all ages, but most by the young and the old. Borrowing is the most common use, but it is not the only one, and the other uses — meeting, asking, sitting, keeping warm — are named by a quarter to a third of users, and are named as the most important use by a substantial minority. The loss, if the library closed, would fall hardest on those with the least: the poor, the old, the young, and those without transport. The library is a public good, and its value cannot be measured by borrowing figures alone, because the borrowing figures count only the books, and the library is more than the books.\n\nThe finding that the average user named 2.6 uses is the study\'s most important result. It shows that the library is not a single service, but a bundle of services, and that the bundle is the point. A user who borrows books, and uses the computer, and meets a friend, is using the library in three ways, and the three ways support each other: the friend tells the user about a book, the book leads the user to the computer, the computer leads the user to a form, the form is filled in with the librarian\'s help. The library is a place where uses combine, and the combination is the value. A library that only lent books would be a smaller thing, and a less valuable thing, than the library that lends books, and gives help, and gives warmth, and gives company, in the same room.\n\nThe finding that 11 per cent of users named keeping warm, all of them older adults, in the winter, deserves attention. It is a small figure, and it is a human figure. An older person, living alone, in a cold house, comes to the library to be warm, and to be among people, and the library gives both, without asking, and without charging. The borrowing figures will never show this. The visit counts will show that the person came, but not why. The interview shows why, and the why is the library\'s purpose, stated in Ranganathan\'s first law: books are for use, and the library is for use, and the use includes being warm, and being among people, and being welcome. A library that is judged only by its loans will be judged wrongly, and a library that is closed because its loans are low will have taken warmth, and company, and help, away from people who have nowhere else to go.\n\nThe study has limits, and they should be stated plainly. The sample was a sample of users, not of the town, and the study cannot say what proportion of the town uses the library, or why the rest do not. The interviews were short, and the answers were the users\' own words, and the users may have overstated their use, or understated it, or given the answer they thought the interviewer wanted. The study covered six months, and the winter months will have raised the figure for keeping warm, and lowered the figure for other uses. The study covered twelve libraries, in three counties, and the libraries may not represent all small-town libraries, in all places. These limits do not invalidate the findings. They qualify them, and they point to further research: a study of non-users, a study over a full year, a study of more libraries, in more places.\n\nThe practical implications are for the towns, and for those who fund the libraries. The library should be judged by its uses, not only by its loans. The uses should be counted, and the counting should include the meeting, and the help, and the warmth, and the computer, and the programs, and the sitting, and the reading, and the borrowing, all together, because the together is the library. The library should be kept open, in the winter, and in the evenings, and at the weekends, because the users who need it most are the ones who come when it is cold, and when they are free, and the hours are the service. And the library should be staffed, by a librarian who knows the users, and who can help, because the help is the service that no machine can give, and the librarian is the reason the library is more than a room full of books.\n\n5. Conclusion\n\nThe small-town library is used by all ages, for many purposes, and its loss would fall hardest on those with the least. Borrowing books is the most common use, but it is one use among many, and the library\'s value lies in the bundle: the books, and the computer, and the help, and the meeting, and the warmth, and the welcome. The borrowing figures do not capture the value, and the library should not be judged by them alone. The library is a public good, and its goodness is in its use, and its use is in the lives of the people who walk through its door, and who find, inside, what they cannot find anywhere else in the town.\n\nReferences\n\nAmerican Library Association. State of America\'s Libraries Report. Chicago: American Library Association, 2023.\nCarnegie, A. "The Gospel of Wealth." North American Review 148 (1889), pp. 653-664.\nRanganathan, S. R. The Five Laws of Library Science. Madras: Madras Library Association, 1931.\nShera, J. H. Foundations of the Public Library: The Origins of the Public Library Movement in New England, 1629-1855. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1949.\n'

pc = len([p for p in TEXT.split("\n\n") if p.strip()])
rt = -(-wc // 200)
avg = wc / sc if sc else 0
uniq = len({w.strip(".,;:!?\"'()[]").lower() for w in words if w.strip(".,;:!?\"'()[]")})
toks = [w.strip(".,;:!?\"'()[]").lower() for w in words]
stop = set("a an the and or of to in on for with as at by from is was are were be been being it its this that these those he she they we you i his her their our your my me him us them not no but so if then than when while who whom which what how all any some more most other into over under out up down off about after before between through during against without within upon per via".split())
toks = [t for t in toks if len(t) > 3 and t.isalpha() and t not in stop]
top = Counter(toks).most_common(5)
longest = max((w.strip(".,;:!?\"'()[]") for w in words), key=len, default="")
print(f"Title: {TITLE}")
print(f"Words: {wc}")
print(f"Sentences: {sc}")
print(f"Paragraphs: {pc}")
print(f"Reading time at 200 words per minute: {wc} / 200 = {wc / 200:.2f}, rounded up = {rt} minutes")
print(f"Average sentence length: {wc} / {sc} = {avg:.1f} words" if sc else "Average sentence length: no sentences found")
print(f"Unique words: {uniq}")
print(f"Longest word: {longest} ({len(longest)} letters)")
print("Most frequent words (over 3 letters): " + ", ".join(f"{w} ({c})" for w, c in top))

The figures are modest, in absolute terms, and they are the figures that are used to judge the library, and they do not capture the meeting, and the help, and the warmth, which the users named, and which the figures cannot count.\n\n3.4 The librarian\n\nThe interviews also asked about the librarian, and the answers were the warmest in the study. Seventy-one per cent of users said they had asked the librarian for help, at some time, and 58 per cent said they had asked in the last month. The help asked for was of many kinds: finding a book, 44 per cent; using the computer, 31 per cent; filling in a form, 18 per cent; finding information, 22 per cent; and other help, 12 per cent, including writing a letter, reading a letter, and making a telephone call. When asked what the librarian\'s help was worth, 83 per cent said it was very important, 12 per cent said it was fairly important, and 5 per cent said it was not important. The users who said it was very important were disproportionately the older users, and the users without a computer at home, and the users who had been using the library longest.\n\nThe users were also asked what would happen if the librarian were replaced by a machine — by a self-service kiosk, for borrowing, and by a computer, for information. Sixty-eight per cent said the library would be worse, and 21 per cent said it would be much worse. Only 4 per cent said it would be better, and 7 per cent said it would make no difference. The reasons given were consistent: the machine cannot answer a question that the user does not know how to ask, the machine cannot tell the user about a book the user has not thought of, and the machine cannot be kind. The librarian can do all three, and the doing is the service. The library, the users said, is not the books. It is the person who knows the books, and who knows the users, and who puts the two together. The finding is the study\'s most human result, and it is the one that the borrowing figures will never show.\n\n4. Discussion\n\nThe study found what it expected to find, and it found more. The library is used by all ages, but most by the young and the old. Borrowing is the most common use, but it is not the only one, and the other uses — meeting, asking, sitting, keeping warm — are named by a quarter to a third of users, and are named as the most important use by a substantial minority. The loss, if the library closed, would fall hardest on those with the least: the poor, the old, the young, and those without transport. The library is a public good, and its value cannot be measured by borrowing figures alone, because the borrowing figures count only the books, and the library is more than the books.\n\nThe finding that the average user named 2.6 uses is the study\'s most important result. It shows that the library is not a single service, but a bundle of services, and that the bundle is the point. A user who borrows books, and uses the computer, and meets a friend, is using the library in three ways, and the three ways support each other: the friend tells the user about a book, the book leads the user to the computer, the computer leads the user to a form, the form is filled in with the librarian\'s help. The library is a place where uses combine, and the combination is the value. A library that only lent books would be a smaller thing, and a less valuable thing, than the library that lends books, and gives help, and gives warmth, and gives company, in the same room.\n\nThe finding that 11 per cent of users named keeping warm, all of them older adults, in the winter, deserves attention. It is a small figure, and it is a human figure. An older person, living alone, in a cold house, comes to the library to be warm, and to be among people, and the library gives both, without asking, and without charging. The borrowing figures will never show this. The visit counts will show that the person came, but not why. The interview shows why, and the why is the library\'s purpose, stated in Ranganathan\'s first law: books are for use, and the library is for use, and the use includes being warm, and being among people, and being welcome. A library that is judged only by its loans will be judged wrongly, and a library that is closed because its loans are low will have taken warmth, and company, and help, away from people who have nowhere else to go.\n\nThe study has limits, and they should be stated plainly. The sample was a sample of users, not of the town, and the study cannot say what proportion of the town uses the library, or why the rest do not. The interviews were short, and the answers were the users\' own words, and the users may have overstated their use, or understated it, or given the answer they thought the interviewer wanted. The study covered six months, and the winter months will have raised the figure for keeping warm, and lowered the figure for other uses. The study covered twelve libraries, in three counties, and the libraries may not represent all small-town libraries, in all places. These limits do not invalidate the findings. They qualify them, and they point to further research: a study of non-users, a study over a full year, a study of more libraries, in more places.\n\nThe practical implications are for the towns, and for those who fund the libraries. The library should be judged by its uses, not only by its loans. The uses should be counted, and the counting should include the meeting, and the help, and the warmth, and the computer, and the programs, and the sitting, and the reading, and the borrowing, all together, because the together is the library. The library should be kept open, in the winter, and in the evenings, and at the weekends, because the users who need it most are the ones who come when it is cold, and when they are free, and the hours are the service. And the library should be staffed, by a librarian who knows the users, and who can help, because the help is the service that no machine can give, and the librarian is the reason the library is more than a room full of books.\n\n5. Conclusion\n\nThe small-town library is used by all ages, for many purposes, and its loss would fall hardest on those with the least. Borrowing books is the most common use, but it is one use among many, and the library\'s value lies in the bundle: the books, and the computer, and the help, and the meeting, and the warmth, and the welcome. The borrowing figures do not capture the value, and the library should not be judged by them alone. The library is a public good, and its goodness is in its use, and its use is in the lives of the people who walk through its door, and who find, inside, what they cannot find anywhere else in the town.\n\nReferences\n\nAmerican Library Association. State of America\'s Libraries Report. Chicago: American Library Association, 2023.\nCarnegie, A. "The Gospel of Wealth." North American Review 148 (1889), pp. 653-664.\nRanganathan, S. R. THE THERMAL BEHAVIOUR OF A CLAY OVEN: MEASUREMENTS AND A MODEL

Abstract

This study measured the heating and cooling of a clay oven, of the kind used for baking bread, and compared the measurements with a simple model of heat conduction. The oven, a dome of clay 60 centimetres in diameter, was heated by a wood fire, and its temperature was measured at six points, inside and outside the wall, over a period of six hours. The inside face reached 320 degrees Celsius, and the outside face reached 85 degrees, and the oven cooled from 320 to 100 degrees in four hours, after the fire was removed. A one-dimensional conduction model, using the thermal properties of fired clay, predicted the cooling curve to within 8 per cent, and the heating curve to within 12 per cent. The results show that the clay wall acts as a store of heat, releasing it slowly, and that the oven's baking performance depends on the wall's thickness and on its thermal diffusivity. The findings are of practical use to bakers, and to builders of clay ovens, and they illustrate the physics of heat conduction in a familiar object.

1. Introduction

The clay oven is one of the oldest cooking devices in the world. It is a dome of clay, or of brick, with an opening at the front, and a fire inside it, and bread baked on its floor, or on its walls. It has been used for thousands of years, in every continent, and it is still used, because it bakes well: the bread has a crisp crust, and a soft inside, and a flavour that no metal oven gives. The reason it bakes well is thermal, and the thermal reason is the subject of this study. The clay wall stores heat, and releases it slowly, and the slow release is what bakes the bread evenly, without burning it. The study measures the heating and the cooling, and it tests a model, and it asks a practical question: how thick should the wall be, and how hot should the fire be, and how long will the oven stay hot enough to bake?

The physics of the oven is the physics of heat conduction. Heat moves from hot to cold, through the clay, by conduction, and the rate at which it moves depends on the clay's thermal conductivity, and on its density, and on its specific heat, and on the thickness of the wall. The fire heats the inside face, and the heat moves through the wall, to the outside face, and the outside face loses heat to the air, by convection, and by radiation. The oven reaches a steady state, in which the heat in equals the heat out, and the temperature is constant, at every point in the wall. When the fire is removed, the oven cools, and the cooling is governed by the same conduction, in reverse: the heat stored in the wall moves out, to the inside face, and to the outside face, and the temperature falls, slowly, because the clay holds a great deal of heat, and releases it slowly.

The study was designed to measure this behaviour, and to test a model of it. The model is deliberately simple: one-dimensional conduction through a flat wall, with the thermal properties of fired clay, and with convective loss from the outside face. A dome is not a flat wall, and the model is an approximation, and the study tests how good the approximation is. The hypothesis was that the model would predict the cooling curve well, because cooling is dominated by conduction, and would predict the heating curve less well, because heating is complicated by the fire, and by radiation, and by the unevenness of the flame. The study also measured the effect of wall thickness, by comparing the oven with a thinner-walled oven, of the same diameter, to test the practical question of how thick the wall should be.

1.1 Previous research

The science of heat began with Newton, who in 1701 published his scale of temperatures, and his law of cooling: that the rate at which a body cools is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the temperature of its surroundings. Newton's law is the foundation of this study, because the oven's cooling follows it, approximately, and the departures from it show where the simple law fails, and where conduction matters. Fourier, in 1822, gave the theory its mathematical form: the heat equation, which describes how temperature changes, in space and in time, in a conducting solid. Fourier's equation is the model used here, in its one-dimensional form, and the study is, in effect, a test of Fourier's equation, in a clay dome, over six hours.

The modern textbook account is given by Incropera and DeWitt, in their Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, which sets out the thermal properties of materials, including fired clay, and the methods for solving the heat equation, for simple geometries, and for simple boundary conditions. The properties used here — thermal conductivity 0.8 watts per metre per kelvin, density 1,800 kilograms per cubic metre, specific heat 880 joules per kilogram per kelvin — are taken from that account, and from the measurements reported there, for clay brick, which is the closest standard material to the clay of the oven. The study's contribution is not new theory. It is the application of the theory to a familiar object, and the measurement of how well the theory does, in practice, with real clay, and a real fire.

2. Methods

2.1 The ovens

Two ovens were built for the study, both domes of clay, 60 centimetres in internal diameter, with a circular opening at the front, 25 centimetres in diameter, and a flat clay floor. The first oven, Oven A, had a wall 8 centimetres thick. The second oven, Oven B, had a wall 4 centimetres thick. Both ovens were built of the same clay, mixed with sand and straw, in the traditional manner, and were dried for two weeks, and fired, slowly, over three days, before the measurements began. The ovens stood outdoors, on a brick base, sheltered from wind by a low wall, and the measurements were made on calm days, with an air temperature between 15 and 18 degrees Celsius.

2.2 Measurement

Temperature was measured by six thermocouples, in each oven. Three thermocouples were set in the wall, at the crown of the dome: one at the inside face, one at the middle of the wall, and one at the outside face. Two thermocouples measured the air inside the oven, one near the floor and one near the crown. One thermocouple measured the outside air, one metre from the oven, in the shade. The thermocouples were read every ten minutes, by a data logger, and the readings were recorded. The fire was a wood fire, of dry hardwood, built on the floor of the oven, and fed for two hours, until the inside face reached 320 degrees Celsius, and the fire was then removed, and the oven was left to cool, with the opening closed by a clay door, and the cooling was measured for four hours.

2.3 The model

The model was one-dimensional conduction through a flat wall, of thickness L, with thermal conductivity k, density rho, and specific heat c, giving a thermal diffusivity alpha = k / (rho c). The heat equation was solved, for the wall, with the inside face held at the measured inside temperature during heating, and with the outside face losing heat by natural convection, with a heat transfer coefficient of 8 watts per square metre per kelvin, during both heating and cooling. During cooling, the inside face was taken as insulated by the closed door, except for a small loss, and the initial temperature distribution was taken as the measured distribution at the moment the fire was removed. The equation was solved by finite differences, with a spatial step of 1 centimetre and a time step of 10 seconds, and the predicted temperatures at the three wall positions were compared with the measured temperatures.

3. Results

3.1 Heating

In Oven A, the inside face reached 320 degrees Celsius after two hours of firing. The middle of the wall reached 210 degrees, and the outside face reached 85 degrees. The temperature rose fastest in the first hour, and more slowly in the second, as the wall stored heat, and the gradient through the wall grew. The air inside the oven, near the crown, reached 380 degrees, and near the floor, 340 degrees. In Oven B, the thin-walled oven, the inside face reached 320 degrees after one hour and twenty minutes, faster than Oven A, and the outside face reached 140 degrees, much hotter than Oven A's 85, because the thinner wall let the heat through more quickly, and stored less of it.

3.2 Cooling

After the fire was removed, and the door was closed, Oven A cooled from 320 degrees, at the inside face, to 100 degrees in four hours. The cooling was fastest in the first hour, falling 90 degrees, and slower thereafter, falling 60 degrees in the second hour, 40 in the third, and 30 in the fourth, following Newton's law, approximately, with the rate proportional to the difference from the air temperature. The outside face cooled from 85 degrees to 40 degrees in the same four hours. The middle of the wall cooled from 210 to 90 degrees. Oven B cooled faster: from 320 to 100 degrees in two hours and twenty minutes, against Oven A's four hours. The thin wall stored less heat, and released it faster, and the oven was usable for baking for a shorter time.

3.3 The model

The model predicted the cooling of Oven A well. The predicted inside-face temperature was within 8 per cent of the measured temperature, at every point in the four hours, with a mean error of 5 per cent. The predicted middle and outside-face temperatures were within 10 per cent. The model predicted the heating less well: the predicted inside-face temperature was within 12 per cent, but the predicted outside-face temperature was 15 per cent low, in the second hour, because the model did not account for radiation from the fire to the outside of the wall, through the opening, and for the unevenness of the flame. For Oven B, the model predicted the cooling to within 9 per cent, and the heating to within 14 per cent. The model is better at cooling than at heating, as hypothesised, and it is good enough, for practical purposes, to predict how long an oven will stay hot enough to bake.

3.4 The baking window

The measurements were also used to calculate the baking window: the time for which the oven stays hot enough to bake bread. Bread bakes well when the inside face is between 200 and 320 degrees Celsius, and it bakes poorly below 150 degrees, because the crust does not form, and the inside does not set. In Oven A, the inside face stayed above 200 degrees for two hours and forty minutes, after the fire was removed, and above 150 degrees for three hours and twenty minutes. In Oven B, the inside face stayed above 200 degrees for one hour and twenty minutes, and above 150 degrees for one hour and fifty minutes. The thick wall gives almost twice the baking window of the thin wall, and the difference is the difference between baking three batches of bread and baking one. The baker who builds thick, bakes more, and the baker who builds thin, bakes less, and the numbers say so, plainly, in hours and minutes.

The baking window was also measured with the door opened, as it would be in use, when bread is put in and taken out. With the door opened for one minute, every twenty minutes, to simulate the baker's work, Oven A stayed above 200 degrees for two hours and twenty minutes, twenty minutes less than with the door closed, and above 150 degrees for three hours. The openings cost heat, but not much, because the wall stores so much, and the loss through the door is small compared with the store in the wall. The baker need not fear opening the door. The oven will forgive it, and the bread will still bake, as long as the door is closed again, promptly, and the wall is thick.

4. Discussion

The study shows that the clay oven works as a store of heat, and that the store is the wall. The fire heats the wall, and the wall stores the heat, and the wall releases it, slowly, to the inside, where the bread bakes, and to the outside, where it is lost. The thick wall, at 8 centimetres, stores twice as much heat as the thin wall, at 4 centimetres, and it releases it for almost twice as long: four hours, against two hours and twenty minutes, to fall from 320 to 100 degrees. The thick wall is also cooler on the outside, 85 degrees against 140, which means it loses less heat to the air, and is safer to touch, and to stand beside. The practical conclusion is plain: a thick wall is better, for baking, and the extra clay is worth the extra building, because it doubles the baking time, and it halves the loss.

The model shows that the physics is understood. A one-dimensional conduction model, with standard properties for fired clay, predicts the cooling to within 8 per cent, which is good enough for a baker, and for a builder, to plan by. The model is worse at heating, at 12 per cent, because the fire is not a clean boundary condition: it radiates, and it flickers, and it heats unevenly, and the model does not capture that. The heating error is not a failure of the theory. It is a failure of the boundary condition, and it can be improved by measuring the fire's heat flux, directly, rather than by assuming the inside-face temperature. The study's heating measurements, with the inside face reaching 320 degrees in two hours, and the outside face reaching 85, give the builder the numbers needed: the fire must be fed for two hours, for an 8-centimetre wall, and the oven will then bake for four hours, cooling from 320 to 100, which is the range in which bread bakes well.

The study has limits, and they should be stated plainly. The ovens were built of one clay, in one place, and fired in one way, and the results may not generalise to other clays, or to brick ovens, or to ovens heated by gas. The measurements were made on calm days, and wind would increase the outside loss, and shorten the cooling time. The model is one-dimensional, and the dome is three-dimensional, and the curvature will affect the conduction, although the wall is thin compared with the diameter, and the error is small. The study measured temperature, not bread: it did not bake, and it did not taste, and the connection between the temperature curve and the quality of the bread is a matter for the baker, not for the thermometer. These limits do not invalidate the findings. They qualify them, and they point to further work: baking trials, at measured temperatures, and a three-dimensional model, and measurements in wind.

The practical implications are for bakers, and for builders. Build the wall thick — 8 centimetres, or more — and the oven will bake longer, and lose less heat, and be safer. Fire the oven for two hours, until the inside face is 320 degrees, and then close the door, and bake, and the oven will stay above 100 degrees for four hours, which is enough for several batches of bread. Do not open the door often, because every opening lets heat out, and the heat is the baking. And trust the model, for cooling, because it is accurate to within 8 per cent, and 8 per cent is close enough, when the question is whether the oven will still be hot enough, in three hours, to bake the next batch.

4.1 Comparison with a metal oven

It is worth comparing the clay oven with a metal oven, of the same size, because the comparison shows what the clay does that the metal cannot. A metal oven, heated to 320 degrees, cools to 100 degrees in about forty minutes, after the heat is removed, because the metal wall is thin, and it stores little heat, and it loses what it stores quickly, to the air. The clay oven, at 8 centimetres thick, takes four hours to make the same fall. The metal oven must be heated continuously, while it bakes, and the heat must be controlled, moment by moment, or the bread will burn, or will not rise. The clay oven is heated once, and then it bakes, on its stored heat, for hours, without further attention, and the heat falls slowly, and the bread bakes evenly, because the temperature is falling, not rising, and the falling temperature is the right temperature for bread: hot at first, for the crust, and cooler later, for the inside. The metal oven is a machine, and it must be tended. The clay oven is a store, and it tends itself, and the difference is the difference between a device that makes heat, and a device that keeps it.

The comparison also explains the flavour. The bread from a clay oven has a crust that is crisp, and an inside that is soft, and a flavour that is often described as earthy, and the flavour comes, in part, from the slow, falling heat, and in part from the clay itself, which gives off a faint, mineral note, when it is hot, and which the bread takes up, in the hours it spends in the oven. The bread from a metal oven is baked by hot air, and the air is dry, and the crust is hard, and the flavour is plainer. The difference is not a matter of taste alone. It is a matter of physics: of stored heat, against supplied heat, and of a wall that remembers the fire, against a wall that forgets it, the moment the fire is gone.

5. Conclusion

The clay oven stores heat in its wall, and releases it slowly, and the release is governed by conduction, and can be predicted by a simple model, to within 8 per cent for cooling. A wall 8 centimetres thick stays hot enough to bake for four hours, after two hours of firing, and a wall 4 centimetres thick for two hours and twenty minutes. The thick wall is better, and the model is good enough to plan by. The oven is an old device, and its physics is old too — Newton, and Fourier, and the heat equation — and the study shows that the old physics still works, in a clay dome, on a calm day, with a wood fire, and that the bread that comes out of it is baked by conduction, and by patience, and by a wall that remembers the fire, long after the fire is gone.

References

Fourier, J. Théorie analytique de la chaleur. Paris: Firmin Didot, 1822.
Incropera, F. P., and DeWitt, D. P. Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer. New York: John Wiley & Sons, 1981.
Newton, I. "Scala graduum Caloris. Calorum Descriptiones & signa." Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 22 (1701), pp. 824-829.

The results show that the clay wall acts as a store of heat, releasing it slowly, and that the oven\'s baking performance depends on the wall\'s thickness and on its thermal diffusivity. The findings are of practical use to bakers, and to builders of clay ovens, and they illustrate the physics of heat conduction in a familiar object.\n\n1. Introduction\n\nThe clay oven is one of the oldest cooking devices in the world. It is a dome of clay, or of brick, with an opening at the front, and a fire inside it, and bread baked on its floor, or on its walls. It has been used for thousands of years, in every continent, and it is still used, because it bakes well: the bread has a crisp crust, and a soft inside, and a flavour that no metal oven gives. The reason it bakes well is thermal, and the thermal reason is the subject of this study. The clay wall stores heat, and releases it slowly, and the slow release is what bakes the bread evenly, without burning it. The study measures the heating and the cooling, and it tests a model, and it asks a practical question: how thick should the wall be, and how hot should the fire be, and how long will the oven stay hot enough to bake?\n\nThe physics of the oven is the physics of heat conduction. Heat moves from hot to cold, through the clay, by conduction, and the rate at which it moves depends on the clay\'s thermal conductivity, and on its density, and on its specific heat, and on the thickness of the wall. The fire heats the inside face, and the heat moves through the wall, to the outside face, and the outside face loses heat to the air, by convection, and by radiation. The oven reaches a steady state, in which the heat in equals the heat out, and the temperature is constant, at every point in the wall. When the fire is removed, the oven cools, and the cooling is governed by the same conduction, in reverse: the heat stored in the wall moves out, to the inside face, and to the outside face, and the temperature falls, slowly, because the clay holds a great deal of heat, and releases it slowly.\n\nThe study was designed to measure this behaviour, and to test a model of it. The model is deliberately simple: one-dimensional conduction through a flat wall, with the thermal properties of fired clay, and with convective loss from the outside face. A dome is not a flat wall, and the model is an approximation, and the study tests how good the approximation is. The hypothesis was that the model would predict the cooling curve well, because cooling is dominated by conduction, and would predict the heating curve less well, because heating is complicated by the fire, and by radiation, and by the unevenness of the flame. The study also measured the effect of wall thickness, by comparing the oven with a thinner-walled oven, of the same diameter, to test the practical question of how thick the wall should be.\n\n1.1 Previous research\n\nThe science of heat began with Newton, who in 1701 published his scale of temperatures, and his law of cooling: that the rate at which a body cools is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the temperature of its surroundings. Newton\'s law is the foundation of this study, because the oven\'s cooling follows it, approximately, and the departures from it show where the simple law fails, and where conduction matters. Fourier, in 1822, gave the theory its mathematical form: the heat equation, which describes how temperature changes, in space and in time, in a conducting solid. Fourier\'s equation is the model used here, in its one-dimensional form, and the study is, in effect, a test of Fourier\'s equation, in a clay dome, over six hours.\n\nThe modern textbook account is given by Incropera and DeWitt, in their Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, which sets out the thermal properties of materials, including fired clay, and the methods for solving the heat equation, for simple geometries, and for simple boundary conditions. The properties used here — thermal conductivity 0.8 watts per metre per kelvin, density 1,800 kilograms per cubic metre, specific heat 880 joules per kilogram per kelvin — are taken from that account, and from the measurements reported there, for clay brick, which is the closest standard material to the clay of the oven. The study\'s contribution is not new theory. It is the application of the theory to a familiar object, and the measurement of how well the theory does, in practice, with real clay, and a real fire.\n\n2. Methods\n\n2.1 The ovens\n\nTwo ovens were built for the study, both domes of clay, 60 centimetres in internal diameter, with a circular opening at the front, 25 centimetres in diameter, and a flat clay floor. The first oven, Oven A, had a wall 8 centimetres thick. The second oven, Oven B, had a wall 4 centimetres thick. Both ovens were built of the same clay, mixed with sand and straw, in the traditional manner, and were dried for two weeks, and fired, slowly, over three days, before the measurements began. The ovens stood outdoors, on a brick base, sheltered from wind by a low wall, and the measurements were made on calm days, with an air temperature between 15 and 18 degrees Celsius.\n\n2.2 Measurement\n\nTemperature was measured by six thermocouples, in each oven. Three thermocouples were set in the wall, at the crown of the dome: one at the inside face, one at the middle of the wall, and one at the outside face. Two thermocouples measured the air inside the oven, one near the floor and one near the crown. One thermocouple measured the outside air, one metre from the oven, in the shade. The thermocouples were read every ten minutes, by a data logger, and the readings were recorded. The fire was a wood fire, of dry hardwood, built on the floor of the oven, and fed for two hours, until the inside face reached 320 degrees Celsius, and the fire was then removed, and the oven was left to cool, with the opening closed by a clay door, and the cooling was measured for four hours.\n\n2.3 The model\n\nThe model was one-dimensional conduction through a flat wall, of thickness L, with thermal conductivity k, density rho, and specific heat c, giving a thermal diffusivity alpha = k / (rho c). The heat equation was solved, for the wall, with the inside face held at the measured inside temperature during heating, and with the outside face losing heat by natural convection, with a heat transfer coefficient of 8 watts per square metre per kelvin, during both heating and cooling. During cooling, the inside face was taken as insulated by the closed door, except for a small loss, and the initial temperature distribution was taken as the measured distribution at the moment the fire was removed. The equation was solved by finite differences, with a spatial step of 1 centimetre and a time step of 10 seconds, and the predicted temperatures at the three wall positions were compared with the measured temperatures.\n\n3. Results\n\n3.1 Heating\n\nIn Oven A, the inside face reached 320 degrees Celsius after two hours of firing. The middle of the wall reached 210 degrees, and the outside face reached 85 degrees. The temperature rose fastest in the first hour, and more slowly in the second, as the wall stored heat, and the gradient through the wall grew. The air inside the oven, near the crown, reached 380 degrees, and near the floor, 340 degrees. In Oven B, the thin-walled oven, the inside face reached 320 degrees after one hour and twenty minutes, faster than Oven A, and the outside face reached 140 degrees, much hotter than Oven A\'s 85, because the thinner wall let the heat through more quickly, and stored less of it.\n\n3.2 Cooling\n\nAfter the fire was removed, and the door was closed, Oven A cooled from 320 degrees, at the inside face, to 100 degrees in four hours. The cooling was fastest in the first hour, falling 90 degrees, and slower thereafter, falling 60 degrees in the second hour, 40 in the third, and 30 in the fourth, following Newton\'s law, approximately, with the rate proportional to the difference from the air temperature. The outside face cooled from 85 degrees to 40 degrees in the same four hours. The middle of the wall cooled from 210 to 90 degrees. Oven B cooled faster: from 320 to 100 degrees in two hours and twenty minutes, against Oven A\'s four hours. The thin wall stored less heat, and released it faster, and the oven was usable for baking for a shorter time.\n\n3.3 The model\n\nThe model predicted the cooling of Oven A well. The predicted inside-face temperature was within 8 per cent of the measured temperature, at every point in the four hours, with a mean error of 5 per cent. The predicted middle and outside-face temperatures were within 10 per cent. The model predicted the heating less well: the predicted inside-face temperature was within 12 per cent, but the predicted outside-face temperature was 15 per cent low, in the second hour, because the model did not account for radiation from the fire to the outside of the wall, through the opening, and for the unevenness of the flame. For Oven B, the model predicted the cooling to within 9 per cent, and the heating to within 14 per cent. The model is better at cooling than at heating, as hypothesised, and it is good enough, for practical purposes, to predict how long an oven will stay hot enough to bake.\n\n3.4 The baking window\n\nThe measurements were also used to calculate the baking window: the time for which the oven stays hot enough to bake bread. Bread bakes well when the inside face is between 200 and 320 degrees Celsius, and it bakes poorly below 150 degrees, because the crust does not form, and the inside does not set. In Oven A, the inside face stayed above 200 degrees for two hours and forty minutes, after the fire was removed, and above 150 degrees for three hours and twenty minutes. In Oven B, the inside face stayed above 200 degrees for one hour and twenty minutes, and above 150 degrees for one hour and fifty minutes. The thick wall gives almost twice the baking window of the thin wall, and the difference is the difference between baking three batches of bread and baking one. The baker who builds thick, bakes more, and the baker who builds thin, bakes less, and the numbers say so, plainly, in hours and minutes.\n\nThe baking window was also measured with the door opened, as it would be in use, when bread is put in and taken out. With the door opened for one minute, every twenty minutes, to simulate the baker\'s work, Oven A stayed above 200 degrees for two hours and twenty minutes, twenty minutes less than with the door closed, and above 150 degrees for three hours. The openings cost heat, but not much, because the wall stores so much, and the loss through the door is small compared with the store in the wall. The baker need not fear opening the door. The oven will forgive it, and the bread will still bake, as long as the door is closed again, promptly, and the wall is thick.\n\n4. Discussion\n\nThe study shows that the clay oven works as a store of heat, and that the store is the wall. The fire heats the wall, and the wall stores the heat, and the wall releases it, slowly, to the inside, where the bread bakes, and to the outside, where it is lost. The thick wall, at 8 centimetres, stores twice as much heat as the thin wall, at 4 centimetres, and it releases it for almost twice as long: four hours, against two hours and twenty minutes, to fall from 320 to 100 degrees. The thick wall is also cooler on the outside, 85 degrees against 140, which means it loses less heat to the air, and is safer to touch, and to stand beside. The practical conclusion is plain: a thick wall is better, for baking, and the extra clay is worth the extra building, because it doubles the baking time, and it halves the loss.\n\nThe model shows that the physics is understood. A one-dimensional conduction model, with standard properties for fired clay, predicts the cooling to within 8 per cent, which is good enough for a baker, and for a builder, to plan by. The model is worse at heating, at 12 per cent, because the fire is not a clean boundary condition: it radiates, and it flickers, and it heats unevenly, and the model does not capture that. The heating error is not a failure of the theory. It is a failure of the boundary condition, and it can be improved by measuring the fire\'s heat flux, directly, rather than by assuming the inside-face temperature. The study\'s heating measurements, with the inside face reaching 320 degrees in two hours, and the outside face reaching 85, give the builder the numbers needed: the fire must be fed for two hours, for an 8-centimetre wall, and the oven will then bake for four hours, cooling from 320 to 100, which is the range in which bread bakes well.\n\nThe study has limits, and they should be stated plainly. The ovens were built of one clay, in one place, and fired in one way, and the results may not generalise to other clays, or to brick ovens, or to ovens heated by gas. The measurements were made on calm days, and wind would increase the outside loss, and shorten the cooling time. The model is one-dimensional, and the dome is three-dimensional, and the curvature will affect the conduction, although the wall is thin compared with the diameter, and the error is small. The study measured temperature, not bread: it did not bake, and it did not taste, and the connection between the temperature curve and the quality of the bread is a matter for the baker, not for the thermometer. These limits do not invalidate the findings. They qualify them, and they point to further work: baking trials, at measured temperatures, and a three-dimensional model, and measurements in wind.\n\nThe practical implications are for bakers, and for builders. Build the wall thick — 8 centimetres, or more — and the oven will bake longer, and lose less heat, and be safer. Fire the oven for two hours, until the inside face is 320 degrees, and then close the door, and bake, and the oven will stay above 100 degrees for four hours, which is enough for several batches of bread. Do not open the door often, because every opening lets heat out, and the heat is the baking. And trust the model, for cooling, because it is accurate to within 8 per cent, and 8 per cent is close enough, when the question is whether the oven will still be hot enough, in three hours, to bake the next batch.\n\n4.1 Comparison with a metal oven\n\nIt is worth comparing the clay oven with a metal oven, of the same size, because the comparison shows what the clay does that the metal cannot. A metal oven, heated to 320 degrees, cools to 100 degrees in about forty minutes, after the heat is removed, because the metal wall is thin, and it stores little heat, and it loses what it stores quickly, to the air. The clay oven, at 8 centimetres thick, takes four hours to make the same fall. The metal oven must be heated continuously, while it bakes, and the heat must be controlled, moment by moment, or the bread will burn, or will not rise. The clay oven is heated once, and then it bakes, on its stored heat, for hours, without further attention, and the heat falls slowly, and the bread bakes evenly, because the temperature is falling, not rising, and the falling temperature is the right temperature for bread: hot at first, for the crust, and cooler later, for the inside. The metal oven is a machine, and it must be tended. The clay oven is a store, and it tends itself, and the difference is the difference between a device that makes heat, and a device that keeps it.\n\nThe comparison also explains the flavour. The bread from a clay oven has a crust that is crisp, and an inside that is soft, and a flavour that is often described as earthy, and the flavour comes, in part, from the slow, falling heat, and in part from the clay itself, which gives off a faint, mineral note, when it is hot, and which the bread takes up, in the hours it spends in the oven. The bread from a metal oven is baked by hot air, and the air is dry, and the crust is hard, and the flavour is plainer. The difference is not a matter of taste alone. It is a matter of physics: of stored heat, against supplied heat, and of a wall that remembers the fire, against a wall that forgets it, the moment the fire is gone.\n\n5. Conclusion\n\nThe clay oven stores heat in its wall, and releases it slowly, and the release is governed by conduction, and can be predicted by a simple model, to within 8 per cent for cooling. A wall 8 centimetres thick stays hot enough to bake for four hours, after two hours of firing, and a wall 4 centimetres thick for two hours and twenty minutes. The thick wall is better, and the model is good enough to plan by. The oven is an old device, and its physics is old too — Newton, and Fourier, and the heat equation — and the study shows that the old physics still works, in a clay dome, on a calm day, with a wood fire, and that the bread that comes out of it is baked by conduction, and by patience, and by a wall that remembers the fire, long after the fire is gone.\n\nReferences\n\nFourier, J. Théorie analytique de la chaleur. Paris: Firmin Didot, 1822.\nIncropera, F. P., and DeWitt, D. P. Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer. New York: John Wiley & Sons, 1981.\nNewton, I. It is a failure of the boundary condition, and it can be improved by measuring the fire\'s heat flux, directly, rather than by assuming the inside-face temperature. The study\'s heating measurements, with the inside face reaching 320 degrees in two hours, and the outside face reaching 85, give the builder the numbers needed: the fire must be fed for two hours, for an 8-centimetre wall, and the oven will then bake for four hours, cooling from 320 to 100, which is the range in which bread bakes well.\n\nThe study has limits, and they should be stated plainly. The ovens were built of one clay, in one place, and fired in one way, and the results may not generalise to other clays, or to brick ovens, or to ovens heated by gas. The measurements were made on calm days, and wind would increase the outside loss, and shorten the cooling time. The model is one-dimensional, and the dome is three-dimensional, and the curvature will affect the conduction, although the wall is thin compared with the diameter, and the error is small. The study measured temperature, not bread: it did not bake, and it did not taste, and the connection between the temperature curve and the quality of the bread is a matter for the baker, not for the thermometer. These limits do not invalidate the findings. They qualify them, and they point to further work: baking trials, at measured temperatures, and a three-dimensional model, and measurements in wind.\n\nThe practical implications are for bakers, and for builders. Build the wall thick — 8 centimetres, or more — and the oven will bake longer, and lose less heat, and be safer. Fire the oven for two hours, until the inside face is 320 degrees, and then close the door, and bake, and the oven will stay above 100 degrees for four hours, which is enough for several batches of bread. Do not open the door often, because every opening lets heat out, and the heat is the baking. And trust the model, for cooling, because it is accurate to within 8 per cent, and 8 per cent is close enough, when the question is whether the oven will still be hot enough, in three hours, to bake the next batch.\n\n4.1 Comparison with a metal oven\n\nIt is worth comparing the clay oven with a metal oven, of the same size, because the comparison shows what the clay does that the metal cannot. A metal oven, heated to 320 degrees, cools to 100 degrees in about forty minutes, after the heat is removed, because the metal wall is thin, and it stores little heat, and it loses what it stores quickly, to the air. The clay oven, at 8 centimetres thick, takes four hours to make the same fall. The metal oven must be heated continuously, while it bakes, and the heat must be controlled, moment by moment, or the bread will burn, or will not rise. The clay oven is heated once, and then it bakes, on its stored heat, for hours, without further attention, and the heat falls slowly, and the bread bakes evenly, because the temperature is falling, not rising, and the falling temperature is the right temperature for bread: hot at first, for the crust, and cooler later, for the inside. The metal oven is a machine, and it must be tended. The clay oven is a store, and it tends itself, and the difference is the difference between a device that makes heat, and a device that keeps it.\n\nThe comparison also explains the flavour. The bread from a clay oven has a crust that is crisp, and an inside that is soft, and a flavour that is often described as earthy, and the flavour comes, in part, from the slow, falling heat, and in part from the clay itself, which gives off a faint, mineral note, when it is hot, and which the bread takes up, in the hours it spends in the oven. The bread from a metal oven is baked by hot air, and the air is dry, and the crust is hard, and the flavour is plainer. The difference is not a matter of taste alone. It is a matter of physics: of stored heat, against supplied heat, and of a wall that remembers the fire, against a wall that forgets it, the moment the fire is gone.\n\n5. Conclusion\n\nThe clay oven stores heat in its wall, and releases it slowly, and the release is governed by conduction, and can be predicted by a simple model, to within 8 per cent for cooling. A wall 8 centimetres thick stays hot enough to bake for four hours, after two hours of firing, and a wall 4 centimetres thick for two hours and twenty minutes. The thick wall is better, and the model is good enough to plan by. The oven is an old device, and its physics is old too — Newton, and Fourier, and the heat equation — and the study shows that the old physics still works, in a clay dome, on a calm day, with a wood fire, and that the bread that comes out of it is baked by conduction, and by patience, and by a wall that remembers the fire, long after the fire is gone.\n\nReferences\n\nFourier, J.
