BIRDSONG AT DAWN: A CENSUS OF MORNING CHORUS TIMING

Abstract

This study recorded the timing of the dawn chorus — the singing of birds before sunrise — in a mixed woodland, over thirty mornings in spring, to answer three questions: which species sing first, how does the order relate to the time of sunrise, and does the order change with the weather? Twenty-four species were recorded, and the order was consistent: the robin sang first, on average 62 minutes before sunrise, followed by the blackbird, the song thrush, and the wren, with the latest singers, the chaffinch and the goldfinch, beginning 12 minutes before sunrise. The start of singing, for each species, was closely tied to light level, not to clock time, and the whole chorus shifted earlier on clear mornings and later on cloudy ones. The results support the view that the dawn chorus is ordered by the light thresholds of the species, and that the order is a stable feature of the woodland, not an accident of the morning.

1. Introduction

The dawn chorus is one of the most familiar sounds in nature, and one of the least studied, in detail, at a single place, over a season. Every spring, in every woodland, the birds begin to sing before the sun rises, and they sing in an order, and the order is roughly the same, year after year, and the reasons for the order are still debated. The birds sing to defend territory, and to attract mates, and the dawn is the best time to be heard, because the air is still, and the sound carries, and the birds have not yet begun to feed. But why does the robin sing first, and the chaffinch last? Why does the chorus begin an hour before sunrise, and not two hours, or ten minutes? And why does the chorus shift, from day to day, with the weather? These are the questions this study set out to answer, by listening, every morning, for thirty mornings, in one woodland, and by writing down, to the minute, when each species began to sing.

The woodland is a mixed wood, of oak and ash and birch, with an understorey of hazel and hawthorn, on the edge of a village, in the south of England. It is not a large wood — about twelve hectares — but it holds a full complement of common woodland birds, and it has been watched, by the author, for ten years, so that the species present, and their territories, are known. The study was conducted in the spring, from the 15th of April to the 15th of May, when the chorus is at its fullest, and the days are lengthening, and the birds are establishing territories, and seeking mates.

The study's hypothesis was straightforward. The order of singing would be consistent, from day to day, and would be related to the light level at which each species begins to sing: the species that sing first would be those that can see, and sing, in the dimmest light. The start of singing would be tied to light, not to clock time, so that the chorus would begin earlier, relative to sunrise, on clear mornings, when the light comes sooner, and later on cloudy mornings, when it comes later. And the order would not change with the weather, because the order is a property of the species, not of the morning. The study was designed to test these hypotheses, by recording the start of singing, for each species, each morning, together with the light level, the cloud cover, and the temperature.

1.1 Previous research

The study of birdsong is old, and it begins with Darwin, who in The Descent of Man, in 1871, discussed the song of birds as a product of sexual selection: the males sing, and the females choose, and the song evolves, by the choice, toward complexity, and beauty. Darwin's account is the foundation, and it is still, in its essentials, the account used today. The modern work has added the detail: Catchpole and Slater, in 1995, in Bird Song: Biological Themes and Variations, showed that song varies, between species, and within species, and that the variation is related to habitat, and to mating system, and to the need to be heard, in a particular place, at a particular time. Kroodsma, in 2005, in The Singing Life of Birds, showed, by listening, and by recording, over a lifetime, that each species has its own song, and its own way of learning it, and its own time for singing it, and that the dawn chorus is the fullest expression of that life.

The dawn chorus itself has been studied, but rarely in the detail attempted here. Most studies have recorded the chorus for a few mornings, or have recorded only the commonest species, or have not measured the light level. The present study records twenty-four species, over thirty mornings, with light, cloud, and temperature measured each morning, so that the order, and its causes, can be examined together. The study's contribution is the census: a complete record, for one wood, for one spring, of when each species begins to sing, and how the beginning moves, with the light, and with the weather.

2. Methods

2.1 The site

The study site was a mixed deciduous woodland of about twelve hectares, on flat ground, at an altitude of 80 metres, on the edge of a village. The canopy was oak, ash, and birch, with an understorey of hazel, hawthorn, and bramble. The wood was surrounded by fields, on three sides, and by the village, on the fourth. The wood held territories of all the species recorded, and the territories were mapped, by the author, in the spring before the study, by observing singing males, and by noting the boundaries between them.

2.2 Recording

Observations were made every morning, from the 15th of April to the 15th of May, thirty mornings in all. The observer arrived at the wood ninety minutes before sunrise, and stood at a fixed point, in the centre of the wood, and listened, and recorded, in a notebook, the time at which each species was first heard to sing. A species was counted as singing when a male gave a full song, not a call, and not a fragment. The time was recorded to the minute, by a watch, checked daily against the radio time signal. Sunrise time, for each morning, was taken from the published tables for the latitude. Cloud cover was estimated, in eighths, at the start of the observation. Temperature was read from a thermometer, in the shade, at the start. Light level was measured by a light meter, held at the observation point, facing the eastern sky, at ten-minute intervals, from ninety minutes before sunrise until sunrise.

2.3 Analysis

For each species, the mean start time, relative to sunrise, was calculated, over the thirty mornings, together with the standard deviation, and the range. The order of species was determined by the mean start time, earliest first. The relationship between start time and light level was examined by noting the light level at the moment each species began to sing, and by calculating the mean light level for each species. The effect of cloud cover was examined by comparing the mean start time on clear mornings (cloud cover 0 to 2 eighths) with the mean start time on cloudy mornings (6 to 8 eighths), for the five earliest species, and for the chorus as a whole. The level of significance was set at p < .05, and all tests were two-tailed.

3. Results

3.1 The order

Twenty-four species were recorded. The order, by mean start time relative to sunrise, was as follows. The robin sang first, at a mean of 62 minutes before sunrise (standard deviation 6 minutes, range 50 to 74). The blackbird followed, at 55 minutes (standard deviation 5, range 45 to 66). The song thrush followed, at 48 minutes (standard deviation 6, range 38 to 60). The wren followed, at 43 minutes (standard deviation 5, range 34 to 53). The dunnock followed, at 38 minutes (standard deviation 6, range 28 to 49). The chaffinch and the goldfinch sang last, at a mean of 12 minutes before sunrise (chaffinch: standard deviation 4, range 5 to 20; goldfinch: standard deviation 5, range 4 to 21). Between the wren and the chaffinch, in order, came the great tit (35 minutes), the blue tit (33), the coal tit (31), the nuthatch (29), the treecreeper (27), the chiffchaff (25), the willow warbler (23), the blackcap (21), the garden warbler (19), the whitethroat (18), the woodpigeon (17), the collared dove (16), the jackdaw (15), the magpie (14), the jay (13), and the greenfinch (12). The order was consistent: the robin was first on 28 of the 30 mornings, and the blackbird was second on 26, and the chaffinch and goldfinch were last on 27.

3.2 Light level

The light level at which each species began to sing was consistent, and it explained the order. The robin began to sing at a mean light level of 0.8 lux (standard deviation 0.2). The blackbird began at 1.5 lux. The song thrush at 2.4 lux. The wren at 3.1 lux. The chaffinch began at 12.5 lux, and the goldfinch at 13.1 lux. The light levels rose steadily through the order, and the correlation between mean start time and mean light level, across the twenty-four species, was r = -.94, p < .001. The earlier a species sang, the dimmer the light at which it sang. The order is an order of light thresholds: the robin can sing in the dimmest light, and the goldfinch needs the brightest.

3.3 Weather

Cloud cover shifted the chorus, but did not change its order. On clear mornings, the robin began at a mean of 68 minutes before sunrise. On cloudy mornings, it began at 56 minutes before sunrise, a difference of 12 minutes, which was significant (t = 4.21, p < .001). The blackbird showed the same pattern: 61 minutes before sunrise on clear mornings, 50 on cloudy, a difference of 11 minutes (t = 3.87, p < .001). The chaffinch showed it too: 16 minutes before sunrise on clear mornings, 9 on cloudy, a difference of 7 minutes (t = 2.94, p = .006). The whole chorus shifted earlier on clear mornings, and later on cloudy ones, by about ten minutes, because the light came sooner on clear mornings, and later on cloudy ones. The order did not change: the robin was first, on clear mornings and on cloudy, and the chaffinch and goldfinch were last, on both. Temperature had no significant effect on start time, when light level was controlled (r = .08, p = .67).

3.4 The full chorus

The study also recorded the time at which the full chorus was reached: the moment when all twenty-four species were singing together. On average, the full chorus was reached 8 minutes before sunrise (standard deviation 4 minutes, range 16 minutes before to 1 minute after sunrise). On clear mornings, the full chorus was reached 11 minutes before sunrise. On cloudy mornings, it was reached 5 minutes before sunrise. The full chorus lasted, on average, 42 minutes, from its start until the first species stopped singing, which was usually the robin, at 34 minutes after sunrise, followed by the wren, and the dunnock. The peak of the chorus — the moment of greatest song, when the most birds were singing at once, and loudest — occurred at a mean of 6 minutes after sunrise, and it was the moment the wood was fullest of sound, and the listener who wants the fullest chorus should be in the wood at sunrise, and should stay for half an hour, and will hear the wood at its best.

The full chorus is a different measure from the first song, and it behaves differently. The first song is ordered by light, species by species. The full chorus is ordered by the latest singer, and the latest singer is the goldfinch, at 12 minutes before sunrise, and the full chorus cannot begin until the goldfinch begins, and so the full chorus begins when the last bird joins, and it ends when the first bird leaves, and the window between them — about forty minutes — is the chorus itself, and it is the part of the morning that the listener remembers, because it is the part when the wood is all singing, at once, and the sound is everywhere, and it is the sound of the wood, awake, and alive.

4. Discussion

The study found what it set out to find: the dawn chorus has a stable order, the order is explained by light, and the order does not change with the weather, although the timing does. The robin sings first, at 62 minutes before sunrise, in light of 0.8 lux. The goldfinch sings last, at 12 minutes before sunrise, in light of 13.1 lux. Between them, twenty-two other species sing, in an order that is consistent from day to day, and that follows the light, step by step, from dim to bright. The correlation between start time and light level, across species, is -.94, which is as close to perfect as field data ever gets, and it leaves little doubt: the chorus is ordered by the light thresholds of the species.

The finding makes sense, in terms of the birds' lives. The robin, which sings first, is a bird that feeds on the ground, in the half-light, and that can see, and sing, when other birds cannot. The blackbird, which sings second, is also a ground feeder, and a bird of the half-light. The finches, which sing last, are birds of the canopy, and of the bright light, and they need more light to see, and to sing. The order is not a matter of who is keenest, or who is loudest. It is a matter of who can see, and the seeing is a matter of the eye, and the eye is a matter of the species. The chorus is the woodland, waking up, in the order in which its birds can see to wake.

The weather finding confirms the light account, and it rules out the clock account. If the birds sang by clock time — by an internal rhythm, set to sunrise — then the chorus would begin at the same time, relative to sunrise, on clear mornings and on cloudy ones. It does not. It begins earlier on clear mornings, and later on cloudy ones, by about ten minutes, because the light comes sooner, and later. The birds are not watching the clock. They are watching the light, and the light is the trigger, and the trigger is the same, for every species, at its own threshold. The order is stable, because the thresholds are stable. The timing shifts, because the light shifts, with the cloud.

The study has limits, and they should be stated plainly. It was conducted in one wood, in one spring, and the order may differ in other woods, and in other springs, although the order found here agrees, in its broad outline, with the orders reported by other observers, in other places: the robin first, the blackbird early, the finches late. The study measured light at a single point, in the centre of the wood, and the light will differ, in different parts of the wood, and the birds in the darker parts may sing later, than the birds in the lighter parts. The study recorded the first song, not the full chorus, and the full chorus — the time when all species are singing together — is a different measure, and it may behave differently. The study did not measure the intensity of the song, or its duration, or its function, and the question of why the birds sing at dawn, and not at noon, is a question for another study, although the answer — that the air is still, and the sound carries, and the birds have not yet begun to feed — is well established in the literature.

The practical implications are for the listener, and for the watcher. The dawn chorus can be predicted, to the minute, for a given wood, on a given morning, if the light is known, and the prediction is a guide to the woodland, and to its birds. The listener who wants to hear the robin should be in the wood an hour before sunrise. The listener who wants to hear the goldfinch can come half an hour later, and will not miss it. The listener who comes on a cloudy morning should come ten minutes later than on a clear one, and will hear the same order, shifted later, like a piece of music played a little slower, but with the same notes, in the same order. The chorus is a clock, and the clock is the light, and the light is the sun, and the sun is the oldest clock there is.

5. Conclusion

The dawn chorus, in a mixed woodland, in spring, has a stable order, from the robin, 62 minutes before sunrise, to the chaffinch and the goldfinch, 12 minutes before sunrise. The order is explained by the light level at which each species begins to sing, from 0.8 lux for the robin to 13.1 lux for the goldfinch, with a correlation of -.94 between start time and light level. The chorus shifts earlier on clear mornings and later on cloudy ones, by about ten minutes, because the light comes sooner and later, but the order does not change. The dawn chorus is ordered by light, and it is stable, and it is predictable, and it is the woodland, waking, in the order in which its birds can see.

References

Catchpole, C. K., and Slater, P. J. B. Bird Song: Biological Themes and Variations. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1995.
Darwin, C. The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex. London: John Murray, 1871.
Kroodsma, D. E. The Singing Life of Birds: The Art and Science of Listening to Birdsong. Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 2005.

The observer arrived at the wood ninety minutes before sunrise, and stood at a fixed point, in the centre of the wood, and listened, and recorded, in a notebook, the time at which each species was first heard to sing. The blackbird followed, at 55 minutes (standard deviation 5, range 45 to 66). The song thrush followed, at 48 minutes (standard deviation 6, range 38 to 60). The wren followed, at 43 minutes (standard deviation 5, range 34 to 53). The dunnock followed, at 38 minutes (standard deviation 6, range 28 to 49). The chaffinch and the goldfinch sang last, at a mean of 12 minutes before sunrise (chaffinch: standard deviation 4, range 5 to 20; goldfinch: standard deviation 5, range 4 to 21). Discussion\n\nThe study found what it set out to find: the dawn chorus has a stable order, the order is explained by light, and the order does not change with the weather, although the timing does. The robin, which sings first, is a bird that feeds on the ground, in the half-light, and that can see, and sing, when other birds cannot. The blackbird, which sings second, is also a ground feeder, and a bird of the half-light. The finches, which sing last, are birds of the canopy, and of the bright light, and they need more light to see, and to sing. The order is not a matter of who is keenest, or who is loudest. It is a matter of who can see, and the seeing is a matter of the eye, and the eye is a matter of the species. The chorus is the woodland, waking up, in the order in which its birds can see to wake.\n\nThe weather finding confirms the light account, and it rules out the clock account. They are watching the light, and the light is the trigger, and the trigger is the same, for every species, at its own threshold. The order is stable, because the thresholds are stable. print(f"Title: {TITLE}")

print(f"Unique words: {uniq}")
print(f"Longest word: {longest} ({len(longest)} letters)")

The listener who comes on a cloudy morning should come ten minutes later than on a clear one, and will hear the same order, shifted later, like a piece of music played a little slower, but with the same notes, in the same order. The chorus is a clock, and the clock is the light, and the light is the sun, and the sun is the oldest clock there is.\n\n5. Conclusion\n\nThe dawn chorus, in a mixed woodland, in spring, has a stable order, from the robin, 62 minutes before sunrise, to the chaffinch and the goldfinch, 12 minutes before sunrise. The order is explained by the light level at which each species begins to sing, from 0.8 lux for the robin to 13.1 lux for the goldfinch, with a correlation of -.94 between start time and light level. The chorus shifts earlier on clear mornings and later on cloudy ones, by about ten minutes, because the light comes sooner and later, but the order does not change. The dawn chorus is ordered by light, and it is stable, and it is predictable, and it is the woodland, waking, in the order in which its birds can see.\n\nReferences\n\nCatchpole, C. K., and Slater, P. J. B. Bird Song: Biological Themes and Variations. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1995.\nDarwin, C. The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex. London: John Murray, 1871.\nKroodsma, D. E. The Singing Life of Birds: The Art and Science of Listening to Birdsong. Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 2005.\n"

THE GROWTH OF BEAN SEEDLINGS UNDER THREE LIGHT REGIMES: AN EXPERIMENTAL STUDY

Abstract

This study measured the growth of bean seedlings under three light regimes — full daylight, shade, and darkness — over fourteen days, to answer three questions: how does light affect the rate of growth, how does it affect the form of the seedling, and how does it affect the colour of the leaves? Ninety seedlings of the common bean, Phaseolus vulgaris, were grown, thirty under each regime, and were measured daily for stem height, and at the end of the experiment for stem height, leaf area, leaf colour, and dry weight. Seedlings in full daylight grew slowest in height, but had the largest leaves, the greenest colour, and the greatest dry weight. Seedlings in darkness grew tallest, but had the smallest leaves, no green colour, and the least dry weight. Seedlings in shade were intermediate, in every measure. The results show that light inhibits stem elongation, and promotes leaf expansion, greening, and the accumulation of dry matter, and they illustrate the plant's response to its light environment, in a form that can be measured, in a school laboratory, in two weeks.

1. Introduction

A seedling, grown in the dark, is a strange thing. It is tall, and pale, and thin, and its leaves are small, and yellow, and folded, and it looks like a plant that has never seen the sun, because it has not. A seedling, grown in the light, is a different thing: shorter, and stouter, and green, with leaves spread wide, and it looks like a plant. The difference is the work of light, and light does more than let the plant see. It shapes the plant, and the shaping is the subject of this study. The study asks a simple question: what does light do to a growing bean seedling, and how much does it do, and can the doing be measured?

The question is old, and it is practical. Every gardener knows that seedlings grown in the dark grow tall and weak, and that seedlings grown in the light grow short and strong, and that the strong seedling is the one that survives, when it is planted out. Every farmer knows that shade changes a crop, and that the change can be measured, in height, and in yield. But knowing that light matters is not the same as knowing how much it matters, or in which direction, for each part of the plant. The stem, the leaf, the colour, the weight — each responds differently, and the study measures each, separately, so that the response can be described, in numbers, and not only in words.

The study's hypothesis was straightforward. Light would inhibit stem elongation: the seedlings in the dark would grow tallest, and the seedlings in full daylight would grow shortest, because light tells the stem to stop growing up, and to grow out, instead. Light would promote leaf expansion: the seedlings in daylight would have the largest leaves, and the seedlings in darkness the smallest, because the leaf is the organ of light, and it grows where light is. Light would promote greening: the seedlings in daylight would be green, and the seedlings in darkness would be yellow, because the green pigment, chlorophyll, is made in the light. And light would promote the accumulation of dry weight: the seedlings in daylight would weigh most, when dried, because they photosynthesise, and the seedlings in darkness would weigh least, because they live on the seed's stored food, and the food runs out. The shade seedlings would be intermediate, in every measure.

1.1 Previous research

The study of plants and light begins with Darwin, who in The Power of Movement in Plants, in 1880, showed that seedlings bend toward light, and that the bending is controlled by the tip of the seedling, and that the tip sends a signal down the stem. Darwin's work is the foundation, and it is still, in its essentials, the account used today. Mendel, in 1866, in his Experiments on Plant Hybridisation, showed that the characters of plants — including their height, and their colour — are inherited, in regular proportions, and that the inheritance can be measured, by counting. Mendel's work is the foundation of genetics, and it is the reason the study uses a single variety, of a single species, so that the differences measured are differences of light, not of inheritance.

Sachs, in 1887, in his Lectures on the Physiology of Plants, set out the physiology of growth: that the plant grows by the division and the expansion of cells, and that the expansion depends on water, and on light, and on temperature, and that the plant's form is the result of these factors, acting together. Sachs showed that a seedling grown in the dark — an etiolated seedling, as it is called — grows tall, because its cells expand, lengthwise, without the check that light imposes, and that the etiolation is reversed, when the seedling is brought into the light, and the leaves expand, and the stem shortens, and the green appears. The present study is, in effect, a measurement of Sachs's description, in numbers, over fourteen days, under three light regimes, with the common bean.

2. Methods

2.1 Plants and conditions

Ninety seeds of the common bean, Phaseolus vulgaris, variety 'Canadian Wonder', were used. The seeds were soaked in water for twelve hours, and were then planted, one per pot, in pots 10 centimetres in diameter, filled with a standard potting compost, and watered. The pots were divided, at random, into three groups of thirty, one group for each light regime. The full-daylight group was placed on a bench in a greenhouse, in natural daylight, with a mean daily light integral of 12 moles per square metre per day. The shade group was placed on the same bench, under a shade cloth that transmitted 30 per cent of the daylight, giving a mean daily light integral of 3.6 moles per square metre per day. The darkness group was placed in a light-tight cupboard, in the same greenhouse, so that the temperature was the same, and was given no light at all. The temperature in the greenhouse was 20 degrees Celsius, by day, and 16 degrees by night, for all groups. The pots were watered daily, with the same amount of water, and were rotated daily, within their group, so that position did not affect the results.

2.2 Measurement

Stem height was measured daily, from the soil surface to the tip of the shoot, with a ruler, to the nearest millimetre, for fourteen days, from the day the shoot emerged from the soil. At the end of the fourteen days, the seedlings were harvested, and four further measures were taken. Leaf area was measured by tracing each leaf on graph paper, and counting the squares, and adding the areas, for all the leaves of the seedling. Leaf colour was measured by matching the largest leaf against a standard colour chart, on a scale from 1 (yellow) to 5 (dark green), by two observers, independently, and the scores were averaged. Dry weight was measured by drying the whole seedling, above ground, in an oven at 80 degrees Celsius, for 48 hours, and weighing it, to the nearest 0.01 grams. The number of leaves was also counted.

2.3 Analysis

Stem height, leaf area, leaf colour, and dry weight were compared across the three light regimes, by one-way analysis of variance, with light regime as the between-groups factor. Pairwise comparisons were made with the Tukey test. The daily height measurements were plotted, and the growth rate, in millimetres per day, was calculated for the period from day 4 to day 14, when growth was linear. The level of significance was set at p < .05, and all tests were two-tailed.

3. Results

3.1 Stem height

Stem height differed clearly between the regimes, from the fourth day onwards. At day 14, the mean height of the full-daylight seedlings was 18.4 centimetres (standard deviation 2.1). The shade seedlings were 26.7 centimetres (standard deviation 2.8). The darkness seedlings were 38.2 centimetres (standard deviation 3.4). Analysis of variance showed a significant main effect of light regime, F(2, 87) = 412.6, p < .001, and all pairwise comparisons were significant (all p < .001). The darkness seedlings were more than twice as tall as the daylight seedlings, and the shade seedlings were intermediate. The growth rate, from day 4 to day 14, was 1.1 millimetres per day for daylight, 1.9 for shade, and 3.2 for darkness. Light inhibited stem elongation, in proportion to its intensity, and the inhibition was orderly: the more light, the shorter the stem.

3.2 Leaves

Leaf area differed in the opposite direction. At day 14, the mean total leaf area of the full-daylight seedlings was 42.6 square centimetres (standard deviation 5.2). The shade seedlings had 28.4 square centimetres (standard deviation 4.1). The darkness seedlings had 6.8 square centimetres (standard deviation 1.9). Analysis of variance showed a significant main effect, F(2, 87) = 521.3, p < .001, and all pairwise comparisons were significant (all p < .001). The daylight seedlings had leaves more than six times the area of the darkness seedlings. The number of leaves also differed: the daylight seedlings had a mean of 6.2 leaves, the shade seedlings 5.1, and the darkness seedlings 2.8, all with small standard deviations, and all pairwise comparisons significant (p < .001). Light promoted leaf expansion, and leaf number, in proportion to its intensity.

3.3 Colour and dry weight

Leaf colour differed clearly. The daylight seedlings scored a mean of 4.6 on the 1-to-5 colour scale (standard deviation 0.4). The shade seedlings scored 3.4 (standard deviation 0.5). The darkness seedlings scored 1.2 (standard deviation 0.3), yellow, with no green. Analysis of variance showed a significant main effect, F(2, 87) = 638.9, p < .001, and all pairwise comparisons were significant (all p < .001). Dry weight differed in the same direction. The daylight seedlings had a mean dry weight of 1.84 grams (standard deviation 0.21). The shade seedlings had 1.12 grams (standard deviation 0.18). The darkness seedlings had 0.62 grams (standard deviation 0.11). Analysis of variance showed a significant main effect, F(2, 87) = 389.4, p < .001, and all pairwise comparisons were significant (all p < .001). The daylight seedlings weighed almost three times as much, dry, as the darkness seedlings. Light promoted greening, and the accumulation of dry matter, in proportion to its intensity.

3.4 The reversal

A further observation was made, after the fourteen days, on ten seedlings from the darkness group. The ten seedlings were moved into full daylight, and were measured for a further seven days, to see whether the etiolation could be reversed. The reversal was rapid, and it was visible. Within twenty-four hours, the leaves, which had been small and yellow and folded, began to open, and to turn green, starting at the edges, and spreading inward. Within forty-eight hours, the colour score had risen from 1.2 to 2.8, on the five-point scale. Within seven days, it had risen to 4.1, close to the daylight seedlings' 4.6. The leaves expanded, from a mean of 6.8 square centimetres to 24.3, in seven days. The stem, which had been growing at 3.2 millimetres a day, slowed, to 1.4 millimetres a day, close to the daylight rate of 1.1. The seedling did not shrink — a stem, once grown, cannot ungrow — but it stopped growing tall, and it began to grow wide, and green, and the plant that had been a pale, tall thread became, in a week, a short, green plant, with leaves spread to the light.

The reversal shows that etiolation is not damage. It is a strategy, and the strategy is reversible. The seedling in the dark grows tall, to find the light, and when it finds the light, it stops growing tall, and it begins to use the light, and the using is the greening, and the leaf expansion, and the accumulation of weight. The strategy is the plant's answer to the problem of germination underground, in the dark, where the seedling must grow up, through the soil, to the light, before it can photosynthesise, and the growing up must be fast, and the leaves must wait, until the light is reached. The bean seedling is a demonstration of that strategy, in two weeks, in a pot, and the reversal, in a further week, is the demonstration's second half: that the plant knows what to do, when the light comes, and it does it, promptly, and completely.

4. Discussion

The study found what it set out to find, and it found it clearly. Light inhibits stem elongation, and promotes leaf expansion, greening, and the accumulation of dry weight, and the effects are orderly, and proportional to the light. The darkness seedlings were tallest, at 38.2 centimetres, but had the smallest leaves, at 6.8 square centimetres, no green colour, at 1.2 on the scale, and the least dry weight, at 0.62 grams. The daylight seedlings were shortest, at 18.4 centimetres, but had the largest leaves, at 42.6 square centimetres, the greenest colour, at 4.6, and the greatest dry weight, at 1.84 grams. The shade seedlings were intermediate, in every measure. The plant's response to light is not a single response. It is four responses, in different directions, and the directions make sense together: the plant that has light invests in leaves, and in green, and in weight, and it does not need to grow tall, because the light is already there. The plant that has no light invests in height, and in nothing else, because height is the only way to find the light, and the leaves, and the green, and the weight, must wait, until the light is found.

The finding is consistent with the physiology described by Sachs, and with the phototropism described by Darwin. The seedling in the dark elongates, because its cells expand, lengthwise, without the check that light imposes. The check is imposed by light, through the plant's photoreceptors, which signal the stem to stop elongating, and the leaf to expand, and the chlorophyll to form. The signal is proportional to the light, which is why the shade seedlings are intermediate: they receive a third of the light, and they show a third of the response, approximately, in height, and in leaf area, and in colour, and in weight. The proportionality is the study's most useful finding, because it means the response can be predicted, from the light, and the light can be managed, to get the seedling wanted.

The study has limits, and they should be stated plainly. It used one variety, of one species, and the results may not generalise to other varieties, or to other species, although the pattern — etiolation in darkness, and its reversal in light — is general, across flowering plants. It used three light regimes, and the response between them may not be linear, although the three points lie, approximately, on a line, for each measure. It measured the seedlings for fourteen days, and the response over a longer period, or after transplanting, may differ, because the etiolated seedling, brought into the light, will green, and expand its leaves, and slow its stem, and the reversal is itself a subject for study. The study measured the shoot, not the root, and the root's response to light, through the shoot, is a further question. These limits do not invalidate the findings. They qualify them, and they point to further work: more varieties, more regimes, longer periods, and the root.

The practical implications are for gardeners, and for growers, and for teachers. The gardener who grows seedlings in the dark, or in too much shade, will get tall, weak seedlings, with small, yellow leaves, and the seedlings will fail, when planted out, because they have no leaves to photosynthesise with, and no weight to stand on. The gardener who grows seedlings in full daylight will get short, strong seedlings, with large, green leaves, and the seedlings will thrive, because they have the leaves, and the weight, to grow on. The shade is a compromise, and the compromise is visible, in the numbers: the shade seedling is taller than the daylight seedling, and shorter than the darkness seedling, and its leaves are smaller, and its colour is paler, and its weight is less. The gardener's rule is simple: give the seedlings light, and plenty of it, and they will be short, and strong, and green, and they will live. The teacher's rule is the same, and the study is a demonstration that can be done in a school laboratory, in two weeks, with ninety seeds, and three places, and a ruler, and a colour chart, and an oven, and the results will be as clear as they are here, because the plant's response to light is one of the clearest in all of biology.

5. Conclusion

Light shapes the bean seedling, in four measurable ways. It inhibits stem elongation: 18.4 centimetres in full daylight, 26.7 in shade, 38.2 in darkness. It promotes leaf expansion: 42.6 square centimetres in daylight, 28.4 in shade, 6.8 in darkness. It promotes greening: 4.6 on the colour scale in daylight, 3.4 in shade, 1.2 in darkness. And it promotes the accumulation of dry weight: 1.84 grams in daylight, 1.12 in shade, 0.62 in darkness. The shade seedling is intermediate, in every measure, and the response is proportional to the light. The seedling that has light invests in leaves, and in green, and in weight. The seedling that has no light invests in height, and in nothing else, until the light is found. The study measures the difference, and the measurement is the lesson: give the seedling light, and it will grow as a plant should.

References

Darwin, C. The Power of Movement in Plants. London: John Murray, 1880.
Mendel, G. "Versuche über Pflanzenhybriden." Verhandlungen des naturforschenden Vereines in Brünn 4 (1866), pp. 3-47.
Sachs, J. Lectures on the Physiology of Plants. Translated by H. Marshall Ward. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1887.

At the end of the fourteen days, the seedlings were harvested, and four further measures were taken. Dry weight was measured by drying the whole seedling, above ground, in an oven at 80 degrees Celsius, for 48 hours, and weighing it, to the nearest 0.01 grams. Pairwise comparisons were made with the Tukey test. The daily height measurements were plotted, and the growth rate, in millimetres per day, was calculated for the period from day 4 to day 14, when growth was linear. The level of significance was set at p < .05, and all tests were two-tailed.\n\n3. Results\n\n3.1 Stem height\n\nStem height differed clearly between the regimes, from the fourth day onwards. At day 14, the mean height of the full-daylight seedlings was 18.4 centimetres (standard deviation 2.1). The shade seedlings were 26.7 centimetres (standard deviation 2.8). The darkness seedlings were 38.2 centimetres (standard deviation 3.4). Analysis of variance showed a significant main effect of light regime, F(2, 87) = 412.6, p < .001, and all pairwise comparisons were significant (all p < .001). The darkness seedlings were more than twice as tall as the daylight seedlings, and the shade seedlings were intermediate. The growth rate, from day 4 to day 14, was 1.1 millimetres per day for daylight, 1.9 for shade, and 3.2 for darkness. Light inhibited stem elongation, in proportion to its intensity, and the inhibition was orderly: the more light, the shorter the stem.\n\n3.2 Leaves\n\nLeaf area differed in the opposite direction. At day 14, the mean total leaf area of the full-daylight seedlings was 42.6 square centimetres (standard deviation 5.2). The shade seedlings had 28.4 square centimetres (standard deviation 4.1). The darkness seedlings had 6.8 square centimetres (standard deviation 1.9). The number of leaves also differed: the daylight seedlings had a mean of 6.2 leaves, the shade seedlings 5.1, and the darkness seedlings 2.8, all with small standard deviations, and all pairwise comparisons significant (p < .001). The daylight seedlings scored a mean of 4.6 on the 1-to-5 colour scale (standard deviation 0.4). The shade seedlings scored 3.4 (standard deviation 0.5). The darkness seedlings scored 1.2 (standard deviation 0.3), yellow, with no green. The daylight seedlings had a mean dry weight of 1.84 grams (standard deviation 0.21). The shade seedlings had 1.12 grams (standard deviation 0.18). The darkness seedlings had 0.62 grams (standard deviation 0.11). Analysis of variance showed a significant main effect, F(2, 87) = 389.4, p < .001, and all pairwise comparisons were significant (all p < .001). The ten seedlings were moved into full daylight, and were measured for a further seven days, to see whether the etiolation could be reversed. The reversal was rapid, and it was visible. It is a strategy, and the strategy is reversible. The seedling in the dark grows tall, to find the light, and when it finds the light, it stops growing tall, and it begins to use the light, and the using is the greening, and the leaf expansion, and the accumulation of weight. The strategy is the plant\'s answer to the problem of germination underground, in the dark, where the seedling must grow up, through the soil, to the light, before it can photosynthesise, and the growing up must be fast, and the leaves must wait, until the light is reached. The bean seedling is a demonstration of that strategy, in two weeks, in a pot, and the reversal, in a further week, is the demonstration\'s second half: that the plant knows what to do, when the light comes, and it does it, promptly, and completely.\n\n4. Discussion\n\nThe study found what it set out to find, and it found it clearly. Light inhibits stem elongation, and promotes leaf expansion, greening, and the accumulation of dry weight, and the effects are orderly, and proportional to the light. The darkness seedlings were tallest, at 38.2 centimetres, but had the smallest leaves, at 6.8 square centimetres, no green colour, at 1.2 on the scale, and the least dry weight, at 0.62 grams. The daylight seedlings were shortest, at 18.4 centimetres, but had the largest leaves, at 42.6 square centimetres, the greenest colour, at 4.6, and the greatest dry weight, at 1.84 grams. The shade seedlings were intermediate, in every measure. The plant\'s response to light is not a single response. It is four responses, in different directions, and the directions make sense together: the plant that has light invests in leaves, and in green, and in weight, and it does not need to grow tall, because the light is already there. The plant that has no light invests in height, and in nothing else, because height is the only way to find the light, and the leaves, and the green, and the weight, must wait, until the light is found.\n\nThe finding is consistent with the physiology described by Sachs, and with the phototropism described by Darwin. The seedling in the dark elongates, because its cells expand, lengthwise, without the check that light imposes. The check is imposed by light, through the plant\'s photoreceptors, which signal the stem to stop elongating, and the leaf to expand, and the chlorophyll to form. The signal is proportional to the light, which is why the shade seedlings are intermediate: they receive a third of the light, and they show a third of the response, approximately, in height, and in leaf area, and in colour, and in weight. The proportionality is the study\'s most useful finding, because it means the response can be predicted, from the light, and the light can be managed, to get the seedling wanted.\n\nThe study has limits, and they should be stated plainly. It used one variety, of one species, and the results may not generalise to other varieties, or to other species, although the pattern — etiolation in darkness, and its reversal in light — is general, across flowering plants. It used three light regimes, and the response between them may not be linear, although the three points lie, approximately, on a line, for each measure. It measured the seedlings for fourteen days, and the response over a longer period, or after transplanting, may differ, because the etiolated seedling, brought into the light, will green, and expand its leaves, and slow its stem, and the reversal is itself a subject for study. The shade seedling is intermediate, in every measure, and the response is proportional to the light. The seedling that has light invests in leaves, and in green, and in weight. The seedling that has no light invests in height, and in nothing else, until the light is found. The study measures the difference, and the measurement is the lesson: give the seedling light, and it will grow as a plant should.\n\nReferences\n\nDarwin, C. The Power of Movement in Plants. TITLE = 'The Growth of Bean Seedlings Under Three Light Regimes: An Experimental Study'
words = TEXT.split()
wc = len(words)
sc = len(re.findall(r"[.!?]+[\"')\]]*\s", TEXT + " ")) + (1 if re.search(r"[.!?][\"')\]]*\s*$", TEXT.strip()) else 0)
pc = len([p for p in TEXT.split("\n\n") if p.strip()])
rt = -(-wc // 200)
avg = wc / sc if sc else 0
uniq = len({w.strip(".,;:!?\"'()[]").lower() for w in words if w.strip(".,;:!?\"'()[]")})
toks = [w.strip(".,;:!?\"'()[]").lower() for w in words]
stop = set("a an the and or of to in on for with as at by from is was are were be been being it its this that these those he she they we you i his her their our your my me him us them not no but so if then than when while who whom which what how all any some more most other into over under out up down off about after before between through during against without within upon per via".split())
toks = [t for t in toks if len(t) > 3 and t.isalpha() and t not in stop]
top = Counter(toks).most_common(5)
longest = max((w.strip(".,;:!?\"'()[]") for w in words), key=len, default="")
print(f"Title: {TITLE}")
print(f"Words: {wc}")
print(f"Sentences: {sc}")
print(f"Paragraphs: {pc}")
print(f"Reading time at 200 words per minute: {wc} / 200 = {wc / 200:.2f}, rounded up = {rt} minutes")
print(f"Average sentence length: {wc} / {sc} = {avg:.1f} words" if sc else "Average sentence length: no sentences found")
print(f"Unique words: {uniq}")
print(f"Longest word: {longest} ({len(longest)} letters)")
print("Most frequent words (over 3 letters): " + ", ".join(f"{w} ({c})" for w, c in top))
